title: Vows & Contemplations
subtitle: Yoga-sūtra of Patañjali with the Yoga-bhāṣya attributed to Vyāsa
source: English: James Haughton Woods, The Yoga-System of Patañjali (Harvard Oriental Series 17, 1914; public domain). Sanskrit sūtras: sanskritdocuments.org. Vyāsa-bhāṣya (IAST): GRETIL, Ānandāśrama Sanskrit Series 47. Vācaspati's sub-commentary is not included.

entries.title: The five yamas
entries.transliteration: ahiṃsāsatyāsteyabrahmacaryāparigrahā yamāḥ
entries.translation: Abstinence from injury and from falsehood and from theft and from incontinence and from acceptance of gifts are the abstentions.
entries.commentary_en:
Of these [five] abstinence from injury means the abstinence from malice towards all living creatures in every way and at all times. And the other abstentions and observances are rooted in it. In so far as their aim is the perfection of it, they are taught in order to teach it.

And in this sense it has been said, "Surely this same brahman in proportion as he desires to take upon himself many courses-of-action, in this proportion refraining from heedlessly giving injury, fulfils [the abstention of] abstinence from injury in order to give it the full character of its spotlessness." Abstinence-from-falsehood (satya) means speech and mind such as correspond to the object-intended; and speech and mind corresponding to what is seen or inferred or heard.

If speech is spoken in order that one's own knowledge may pass to some one else, it should not be deceitful or mistaken or barren of information; [then it would be abstinence from falsehood]. It should be used for the service of all; not for the ruin of creatures.

And even when used thus, should it be only for the ruin of creatures, it would not be an abstinence from falsehood; it would be nothing less than wrong. In so far as there would be a false kind of merit [and] a resemblance of merit, it would become the worst of evils.

Therefore let [the yogin] consider [first] what is good for all creatures and [then] speak with abstinence-from-falsehood. Theft is the unauthorized (apāstrapūrvaka) appropriation of things-of-value from another. While abstinence-from-theft, when free from coveting, is the refusal to do this. Continence is control of the hidden organ of generation.

Abstinence-from-acceptance-of-gifts is abstinence-from-appropriating objects, because one sees the disadvantages in acquiring them or keeping them or losing them or in being attached to them or in harming them. These then are the abstentions.
entries.commentary_sa:
tatrāhiṃsā sarvathā sarvadā sarvabhūtānām anabhidrohaḥ. uttare ca yamaniyamās tanmūlās tatsiddhiparatayaiva tatpratipādanāya pratipādyante. tadavadātarūpakaraṇāyaivopādīyante. tathā coktam --- sa khalv ayaṃ brāhmaṇo yathā yathā vratāni bahūni samāditsate tathā tathā pramādakṛtebhyo hiṃsānidānebhyo nivartamānas tām evāvadātarūpām ahiṃsāṃ karoti. satyaṃ yathārthe vāṅmanase.

yathā dṛṣṭaṃ yathānumitaṃ tathā vāṅ manaś ceti. paratra svabodhasaṃkrāntaye vāg uktā, sā yadi na vañcitā bhrāntā vā pratipattivandhyā vā bhaved iti. eṣā sarvabhūtopakārārthaṃ pravṛttā na bhūtopaghātāya. yadi caivam apy abhidhīyamānā bhūtopaghātaparaiva syān na satyaṃ bhavet pāpam eva bhavet tena puṇyābhāsena puṇyapratirūpakeṇa kaṣṭaṃ tamaḥ prāpnuyāt.

tasmāt parīkṣya sarvabhūtahitaṃ satyaṃ brūyāt. steyam aśāstrapūrvakaṃ dravyāṇāṃ parataḥ svīkaraṇaṃ, tatpratiṣedhaḥ punar aspṛhārūpam asteyam iti. brahmacaryaṃ guptendriyasyopasthasya saṃyamaḥ. viṣayāṇām arjanarakṣaṇakṣayasaṅgahiṃsādoṣadarśanād asvīkaraṇam aparigraha ity ete yamāḥ.

entries.title: The Great Vow (mahāvrata)
entries.transliteration: jātideśakālasamayānavacchinnāḥ sārvabhaumā mahāvratam
entries.translation: When they are unqualified by species or place or time or exigency and when [covering] all [these] classes — [under these circumstances exists] the Great Course-of-conduct.
entries.commentary_en:
Of these [five], abstinence-from-injury is qualified in respect of species as follows, a catcher of fish does injury to fishes only and to nothing else. — The same is qualified in respect of place, as when one says, 'I will not slay in a holy place.' — The same is qualified in respect of time, as when one says, 'I will not slay on the fourteenth day [of the lunar fortnight] nor on a day of good omen.' — The same, in the case of one who refrains from [these] three is qualified in respect of exigency, as when one says, 'For the sake of gods and brahmans and not otherwise I will slay.' Likewise also in the case of the warrior who says, 'In battle only [I will do] injury, and nowhere else.' Abstinence-from-injury and the other [abstinences] unqualified by these species or times or places or exigencies must be kept when [covering] no less than all [these] cases.

'In all [these] classes' means with regard to all [these] objects. Without exceptions in no less than all [these] classes — this is what is meant by speaking of the Great Course-of-conduct when [covering] all [these] stages.
entries.commentary_sa:
tatrāhiṃsā jātyavacchinnā matsyavadhakasya matsyeṣv eva nānyatra hiṃsā. saiva deśāvacchinnā na tīrthe haniṣyāmīti. saiva kālāvacchinnā na caturdaśyāṃ na puṇye 'hani haniṣyāmīti. saiva tribhir uparatasya samayāvacchinnā devabrāhmaṇārthe nānyathā haniṣyāmīti. yathā ca kṣatriyāṇāṃ yuddha eva hiṃsā nānyatreti.

ebhir jātideśakālasamayair anavacchinnā ahiṃsādayaḥ sarvathaiva paripālanīyāḥ. sarvabhūmiṣu sarvaviṣayeṣu sarvathaivāviditavyabhicārāḥ sārvabhaumā mahāvratam ity ucyante.

entries.title: The five niyamas
entries.transliteration: śaucasaṃtoṣatapaḥsvādhyāyeśvarapraṇidhānāni niyamāḥ
entries.translation: Cleanliness and contentment and self-castigation and study and devotion to the Īśvara are the observances.
entries.commentary_en:
Of these [five], cleanliness is produced by earth or by water or the like, and by the consumption and other [requirements] with regard to pure sacrificial food. This is outer.

Inner [cleanliness] is the washing away of the blemishes of the mind-stuff. — [To practise] contentment means not to covet more than the means at hand. — Self-castigation is the bearing of extremes, hunger and thirst, cold and heat, standing and sitting, stock-stillness and formal stillness, and, according to usage, courses-of-conduct such as mortifications (kṛcchra) and lunar fasts and rigid penances. — Study is the recital of books that treat of release or the repetition of the syllable of adoration (praṇava). — Devotion to the Īśvara is the offering up of all actions to the Supreme Teacher.

"He who rests in himself, for whom the network of perverse-considerations (vitarka) has been destroyed, whether resting upon a bed or on a seat, or wandering upon a road, would behold the destruction of the seed of the round-of-rebirths, would be permanently released, would participate in deathless delights." With regard to which this has been said, [i. 29], "Thereafter comes the right knowledge of him who thinks in an inverse way, and the removal of obstacles."
entries.commentary_sa:
tatra śaucaṃ mṛjjalādijanitaṃ medhyābhyavaharaṇādi ca bāhyam. ābhyantaraṃ cittamalānām ākṣālanam. saṃtoṣaḥ saṃnihitasādhanād adhikasyānupāditsā. tapo dvaṃdvasahanam. dvaṃdvāś ca jighatsāpipāse śītoṣṇe sthānāsane kāṣṭhamaunākāramaune ca. vratāni caiṣāṃ yathāyogaṃ kṛcchracāndrāyaṇasāṃtapanādīni. svādhyāyo mokṣaśāstrāṇām adhyayanaṃ praṇavajapo vā.

īśvarapraṇidhānaṃ tasmin paramagurau sarvakarmārpaṇam. śayyāsanastho 'tha pathi vrajan vā svasthaḥ parikṣīṇavitarkajālaḥ / saṃsārabījakṣayam īkṣamāṇaḥ syān nityayukto 'mṛtabhogabhāgī // yatredam uktaṃ tataḥ pratyakcetanādhigamo 'py antarāyābhāvaś ceti.

entries.title: When contrary thoughts arise
entries.transliteration: vitarkabādhane pratipakṣabhāvanam
entries.translation: If there be inhibition by perverse-considerations (vitarka), there should be cultivation of the opposites.
entries.intro_en: As for these abstentions and observances,
entries.commentary_en:
Whenever [in the mind] of this brahman [practising the abstentions and observances] injuries and similar [faults] arise as perverse-considerations, such as for instance, 'I will kill him who hurts me; I will also lie; I will also appropriate his money; and I will commit adultery with his wife; and I will also make myself master of his property.' Thus inhibited by the blazing fever of perverse-considerations, let him cultivate the opposites of these.

Let him ponder, 'Baked upon the pitiless coals of the round-of-rebirths, I take my refuge in the rules (dharma) for yoga by giving protection to every living creature. I myself after ridding myself of perverse-considerations am betaking myself to them once more, like a dog.

As a dog to his vomit, even so I betake myself to that of which I had rid myself.' Other similar [inhibitions of perverse-considerations] should be applied in the other sutras also [upon the aids to yoga].
entries.commentary_sa:
yadāsya brāhmaṇasya hiṃsādayo vitarkā jāyeran haniṣyāmy aham apakāriṇam anṛtam api vakṣyāmi dravyam apy asya svīkariṣyāmi dāreṣu cāsya vyavāyī bhaviṣyāmi parigraheṣu cāsya svāmī bhaviṣyāmīti. evam unmārgapravaṇavitarkajvareṇātidīptena bādhyamānas tatpratipakṣān bhāvayet. ghoreṣu saṃsārāṅgāreṣu pacyamānena mayā śaraṇam upāgataḥ sarvabhūtābhayapradānena yogadharmaḥ.

sa khalv ahaṃ tyaktvā vitarkān punas tān ādadānas tulyaḥ śvavṛtteneti bhāvayet. yathā śvā vāntāvalehī tathā tyaktasya punar ādadāna iti. evamādi sūtrāntareṣv api yojyam.

entries.title: Contrary thoughts and their consequences
entries.transliteration: vitarkā hiṃsādayaḥ kṛtakāritānumoditā lobhakrodhamohapūrvakā mṛdumadhyādhimātrā duḥkhājñānānantaphalā iti pratipakṣabhāvanam
entries.translation: Since perverse-considerations such as injuries, whether done or caused to be done or approved, whether ensuing upon greed or anger or infatuation, whether mild or moderate or vehement, find their unending consequences in pain and in lack of thinking, there should be the cultivation of their opposites.
entries.commentary_en:
Of these [considerations], first of all, injury, since it is done or caused to be done or approved, is three-fold.

Moreover, each of these is three-fold, in so far as there is greed [such as] desire for the meat or for the skin, or in so far as there is anger as when a man thinks he has been 'hurt by that man', or in so far as there is infatuation as when a man thinks [that what he is doing] 'will be merit for me'.

Again, since greed and anger and infatuation are three-fold as being mild and moderate and vehement, there are thus seven-and-twenty varieties of injuries.

Yet again, since [these are] gentle and moderate and extreme [these are] three-fold as follows, gently mild and moderately mild and keenly mild; similarly, gently moderate and moderately moderate and keenly moderate; likewise, gently keen and moderately keen and vehemently keen. Thus injury is of one-and-eighty varieties.

It is, however, innumerable because of the varieties due to specifications (niyama) and to options (vikalpa) and to aggregations (samuccaya), due to the fact that the varieties of those-who-breathe-the-breath-of-life are innumerable. In the same manner [the classification] is to be applied to falsehood and to the other [crimes].

Now since these perverse considerations have endless consequences in pain and in lack of thinking, one should cultivate their opposites.

[In other words], there is a cultivation of those things the endless consequences of which are pain and a lack of thinking. — And to continue, he who commits an injury first of all reduces the strength of the victim, then causes him pain by falling upon him with a knife or something of the kind, [and] afterwards even deprives him of life.

When once he has taken away [the victim's] strength, his own animate or inanimate aids begin to have their strength dwindle away. As a result of causing pain, he himself experiences pain in hells and in [the bodies of] animals and of departed spirits and in other [forms].

As a result of uprooting [the victim] from life, he himself continues from moment to moment at the very point of departure from life. And even while wishing for death he pants laboriously since the fruition of pain is to be felt in a fruition which has a limit [in time].

Furthermore, even if [the effects of] injury could be somehow done away by merit, even then, if he obtained happiness, it would be [on condition that] his length-of-life be short. — In the same way, so far as possible, [the classification] is to be applied to lying and to the other [violations of the abstentions].

Thus pondering on that same [painful consequence] of perverse considerations, which is inevitable (anugata) and undesired, the yogin should not devote his central organ to perverse considerations. As a result of the cultivation of the opposites, the perverse considerations become things that may be escaped.
entries.commentary_sa:
tatra hiṃsā tāvat --- kṛtā kāritānumoditeti tridhā. ekaikā punas tridhā lobhena māṃsacarmārthena krodhenāpakṛtam aneneti mohena dharmo me bhaviṣyatīti. lobhakrodhamohāḥ punas trividhā mṛdumadhyādhimātrā iti. evaṃ saptaviṃśatir bhedā bhavanti hiṃsāyāḥ. mṛdumadhyādhimātrāḥ punas tridhā --- mṛdumṛdur madhyamṛdus tīvramṛdur iti. tathā mṛdumadhyo madhyamadhyas tīvramadhya iti.

tathā mṛdutīvro madhyatīvro 'dhimātratīvra iti. evam ekāśītibhedā hiṃsā bhavati. sā punar niyamavikalpasamuccayabhedād asaṃkhyeyā, prāṇabhṛdbhedasyāparisaṃkhyeyatvād iti. evam anṛtādiṣv api yojyam. te khalv amī vitarkā duḥkhājñānānantaphalā iti pratipakṣabhāvanam. duḥkham ajñānaṃ cānantaṃ phalaṃ yeṣām iti pratipakṣabhāvanam.

tathā ca hiṃsakas tāvat prathamaṃ vadhyasya vīryam ākṣipati. tataś ca śastrādinipātena duḥkhayati. tato jīvitād api mocayati. tato vīryākṣepād asya cetanācetanam upakaraṇaṃ kṣīṇavīryaṃ bhavati.

duḥkhotpādān narakatiryakpretādiṣu duḥkham anubhavati, jīvitavyaparopaṇāt pratikṣaṇaṃ ca jīvitātyaye vartamāno maraṇam icchann api duḥkhavipākasya niyatavipākavedanīyatvāt kathaṃcid evocchvasiti. yadi ca kathaṃcit puṇyāvāpagatā hiṃsā bhavet tatra sukhaprāptau bhaved alpāyur iti. evam anṛtādiṣv api yojyaṃ yathāsaṃbhavam.

evaṃ vitarkāṇāṃ cāmum evānugataṃ vipākam aniṣṭaṃ bhāvayan na vitarkeṣu manaḥ praṇidadhīta.

entries.title: Ahiṃsā — result
entries.transliteration: ahiṃsāpratiṣṭhāyāṃ tatsaṃnidhau vairatyāgaḥ
entries.translation: As soon as he is grounded in abstinence from injury, his presence begets a suspension of enmity.
entries.intro_en: When [the perverse considerations] become for this [yogin] unsuitable for generation, then the power caused by this fact becomes indicative of the yogin's perfection. For example,
entries.commentary_en: [This] occurs on the part of all living creatures.

entries.title: Satya — result
entries.transliteration: satyapratiṣṭhāyāṃ kriyāphalāśrayatvam
entries.translation: As soon as he is grounded in abstinence from falsehood, actions and consequences depend upon him.
entries.commentary_en: If [the yogin] says to a man (iti), 'Be thou right-living,' the man becomes right-living. If he expresses the wish (iti) 'Attain thou heaven,' the man attains heaven. What he says (vāk) comes true.
entries.commentary_sa: dhārmiko bhūyā iti bhavati dhārmikaḥ, svargaṃ prāpnuhīti svargaṃ prāpnoti amoghāsya vāg bhavati.

entries.title: Asteya — result
entries.transliteration: asteyapratiṣṭhāyāṃ sarvaratnopasthānam
entries.translation: As soon as he is grounded in abstinence from theft, all jewels approach him.
entries.commentary_en: From all directions jewels approach to be his.

entries.title: Brahmacarya — result
entries.transliteration: brahmacaryapratiṣṭhāyāṃ vīryalābhaḥ
entries.translation: As soon as he is grounded in abstinence from incontinence, he acquires energy.
entries.commentary_en: By the acquisition of which the yogin increases [his] unhindered qualities. And when he is perfected he is able to transfer [his] thinking to [his] pupils.
entries.commentary_sa: yasya lābhād apratighān guṇān utkarṣayati. siddhaś ca vineyeṣu jñānam ādhātuṃ samartho bhavatīti.

entries.title: Aparigraha — result
entries.transliteration: aparigrahasthairye janmakathaṃtāsaṃbodhaḥ
entries.translation: As soon as he is established in abstinence-from-acceptance-of-gifts, a thorough illumination upon the conditions of birth —
entries.commentary_en: — Becomes his. 'Who was I? How was I? Or what [can] this birth be? Or how [can] this [birth] be? Or what shall we become? Or how shall we become?' Such a desire to know his own condition in former and later and intermediate times becomes of itself fulfilled for him. These when he is established in the abstentions are the perfections.
entries.commentary_sa: asya bhavati ko 'ham āsaṃ katham aham āsaṃ kiṃsvid idaṃ kathaṃsvid idaṃ ke vā bhaviṣyāmaḥ kathaṃ vā bhaviṣyāma ity evam asya pūrvāntaparāntamadhyeṣv ātmabhāvajijāsā svarūpeṇopāvartate. etā yamasthairye siddhayaḥ.

entries.title: Śauca — result
entries.transliteration: śaucāt svāṅgajugupsā parair asaṃsargaḥ
entries.translation: As a result of cleanliness there is disgust at one's own body and no intercourse with others.
entries.intro_en: We will speak with regard to observances.
entries.commentary_en:
As soon as there is disgust with his own body, he has begun cleanliness. Seeing the offensiveness of the body, he is no longer attached to the body and becomes an ascetic (yati). Moreover there is no intercourse with others.

Perceiving the true nature of the body, desirous of escaping even his own body, even after he has washed it with earth and water and other [substances], not seeing any purity in the body, how could he have intercourse with the bodies of others absolutely unhallowed as they are?
entries.commentary_sa: svāṅge jugupsāyāṃ śaucam ārabhamāṇaḥ kāyāvadyadarśī kāyānabhiṣvaṅgī yatir bhavati. kiṃca parair asaṃsargaḥ kāyasvabhāvāvalokī svam api kāyaṃ jihāsur mṛjjalādibhir ākṣālayann api kāyaśuddhim apaśyan kathaṃ parakāyair atyantam evāprayataiḥ saṃsṛjyeta.

entries.title: Śauca — further results
entries.transliteration: sattvaśuddhisaumanasyaikāgryendriyajayātmadarśanayogyatvāni ca
entries.translation: Purity of sattva and gentleness and singleness-of-intent and subjugation of the senses and fitness for the sight of the self —
entries.commentary_en:
The word 'arise' completes the sentence. As a result of cleanliness there is purity of sattva; therefrom [it acquires] gentleness; from this [it acquires] singleness-of-intent; therefrom [it acquires] subjugation of the senses; and from this fitness for the sight of the self is acquired by the sattva of the thinking-substance.

So to this [last] there is access, as a result of his being established in cleanliness.
entries.commentary_sa: bhavantīti vākyaśeṣaḥ. śuceḥ sattvaśuddhis tataḥ saumanasyaṃ tata aikāgryaṃ tata indriyajayas tataś cātmadarśanayogyatvaṃ buddhisattvasya bhavatīty etac chaucasthairyād adhigamyata iti.

entries.title: Saṃtoṣa — result
entries.transliteration: saṃtoṣād anuttamaḥ sukhalābhaḥ
entries.translation: As a result of contentment there is an acquisition of superlative pleasure.
entries.commentary_en: And in this sense it has been said, "What constitutes the pleasure of love in this world and what the supreme pleasure of heaven are both not to be compared with the sixteenth part of the pleasure of dwindled craving (tṛṣṇā)."
entries.commentary_sa: tathā coktam --- "yac ca kāmasukhaṃ loke yac ca divyaṃ mahat sukham / tṛṣṇākṣayasukhasyaite nārhataḥ ṣoḍaśīṃ kalām" iti.

entries.title: Tapas — result
entries.transliteration: kāyendriyasiddhir aśuddhikṣayāt tapasaḥ
entries.translation: Perfection in the body and in the organs after impurity has dwindled as a result of self-castigation.
entries.commentary_en: Self-castigation in the very act of completing itself destroys the defilement from the covering of impurity. As a result of the removal of the defilement of the covering of this [impurity] there is perfection of the body, such as atomization [iii. 45]; likewise perfection of the organs, such as hearing and seeing at a distance [that is, telepathy].
entries.commentary_sa: nirvartyamānam eva tapo hinasty aśuddhyāvaraṇamalaṃ tadāvaraṇamalāpagamāt kāyasiddhir aṇimādyā. tathendriyasiddhir dūrāc chravaṇadarśanādyeti.

entries.title: Svādhyāya — result
entries.transliteration: svādhyāyād iṣṭadevatāsaṃprayogaḥ
entries.translation: As a result of study there is communion with the chosen deity.
entries.commentary_en: Gods and sages and perfected men come within the range of vision of [the yogin] who has the disposition to study; and are helpful to his work.
entries.commentary_sa: devā ṛṣayaḥ siddhāś ca svādhyāyaśīlasya darśanaṃ gacchanti, kārye cāsya vartanta iti.

entries.title: Īśvarapraṇidhāna — result
entries.transliteration: samādhisiddhir īśvarapraṇidhānāt
entries.translation: Perfection of concentration as a result of devotion to the Īśvara.
entries.commentary_en: One whose whole nature is surrendered to the Īśvara has perfection of concentration. By which [concentration] he knows as the thing really is (avitatham) all that he desires to know, in other places and in other bodies and in other times. Thereafter his insight sees into things as they are (yathābhūtam).
entries.commentary_sa: īśvarārpitasarvabhāvasya samādhisiddhir yayā sarvam īpsitam avitathaṃ jānāti deśāntare dehāntare kālāntare ca. tato 'sya prajñā yathābhūtaṃ prajānātīti.

entries.title: Maitrī · Karuṇā · Muditā · Upekṣā
entries.transliteration: maitrīkaruṇāmuditopekṣāṇāṃ sukhaduḥkhapuṇyāpuṇyaviṣayāṇāṃ bhāvanātaś cittaprasādanam
entries.translation: By the cultivation of friendliness towards happiness and compassion towards pain and joy towards merit and indifference towards demerit [the yogin should attain] the undisturbed calm of the mind-stuff.
entries.intro_en: Of which [stable mind-stuff] this purification is enjoined by the system. By what means is this?
entries.commentary_en:
Of these [four] he should cultivate friendliness towards all living beings that have reached the experience of happiness; compassion towards those in pain; joy towards those whose character is meritorious; indifference towards those whose character is demeritorious. When he thus cultivates [friendliness and the rest] the white quality [of karma] comes into being [within him].

And then the mind-stuff becomes calm; and when calm it becomes single-in-intent and reaches the stable state.
entries.commentary_sa: tatra sarvaprāṇiṣu sukhasaṃbhogāpanneṣu maitrīṃ bhāvayet. duḥkhiteṣu karuṇām. puṇyātmakeṣu muditām. apuṇyaśīleṣūpekṣām. evam asya bhāvayataḥ śuklo dharma upajāyate. tataś ca cittaṃ prasīdati. prasannam ekāgraṃ sthitipadaṃ labhate.

groups.name: Devī Atharvaśīrṣa
groups.subtitleEn: Teachings by Ācārya Sthaneshwar Timalsina, Śrī Devī Atharvaśīrṣa (Vimarsha Publications). English from the book.

entries.title: The Deities Approach Devī
entries.transliteration: oṃ sarve vai devā devīm-upatasthuḥ kāsi tvaṃ mahādevīti || 1 ||
entries.translation: Oṃ. All (sarva) the deities (deva) indeed (vai) approached in worship (upatasthuḥ) toward the Goddess (devī): “Who (kā) are (asi) you (tvam), O Great Goddess (mahādevī)?” [they asked] thus (iti).
entries.intro_en:
Most procedures for prāṇapratiṣṭhā—the installation of life into a mūrti—require only the priest to do the necessary activities. But this procedure we did today is based on the recitation of the Devī Atharvaśīrṣa. Therefore, you could also learn how to perform it. As you can see in the benedictory, in the concluding verses, the text tells you “nūtanāyāṃ pratimāyāṃ japtvā devatāsānnidhyaṃ bhavati”

(“if you recite in front of the new statue, you feel connected”)—and then “prāṇapratiṣṭhāyāṃ japtvā prāṇānāṃ pratiṣṭhā bhavati, ” (“if you recite this text for the prāṇapratiṣṭhā, then it conducts that job as well”). The text gives you a Śākta non-dualism in which the Goddess herself speaks to the deities that: “I am every single thing. I am being and non-being. I am the manifest and unmanifest.

I am the entire world. ” This Devī Atharvaśīrṣa also takes the essence, not all the lines, but major lines from sūktas from the Vedas, like the Vāk Sūkta revealed by the female sage, ṛṣikā Vāk Āmbhṛṇī (“ahaṃ rāṣṭrī saṅgamanī vasūnām cikituṣī prathamā yajñiyānām…”) and the Durgā Sūkta (“tāmagnivarṇāṃ tapasā jvalantīṃ vairocanīṃ karmaphaleṣu juṣṭām…”).

And then it also has the essence of the Devī Sūkta from the Devī Māhātmya (“namo devyai mahādevyai śivāyai satataṃ namaḥ…”). In this text, you will find not just one sūkta alone. You have the combined essence of the Vedic and Purāṇic sūktas. So, this is a really core essential text.

And many of the tantric texts, when they give these sūktas, do not give the whole meditation including how to contemplate upon the nature of the Goddess. This book goes back and forth between mantra, contemplation, and visualization. It spells out the Gāyatrī Teachings on the Devī Atharvaśīrṣa mantra for Mahālakṣmī (“mahālakṣmyai ca vidmahe sarvaśaktyai ca dhīmahi…”). This is the Goddess’s mantra.

One needs to also keep in mind that the Mahālakṣmī invoked here is not the popular Lakṣmī, the consort of Viṣṇu, as Mahālakṣmī stands here as the central deity in the Devī Māhātmya, the Mahiṣāsuramardinī, the Buffalo-slaying Goddess with 18 arms. This book then gives a three-stage sādhanā, where the Goddess reveals herself in three layers of mantra.

One is in the Māyā bīja, hrīṃ, and then the sādhanā course goes into the whole detailed visualization of Bhuvaneśvarī “hṛtpuṇḍarīka-madhyasthāṃ…” (“situated in the middle of the heart, of the form of the sun… ”). The second course of sādhanā comes with “vicce navārṇako’rṇaḥ syānmahadānandadāyakaḥ. ” That is the whole deciphering of the Navārṇa Mantra.

And then the third course goes to give you the Pañcadaśī Śrīvidyā mantra and the visualization of Mahā Tripurasundarī. So this is a three-stage sādhanā itself given in the text. The book then synthesizes the practice of the five mothers, the five goddesses: fitting within the triadic structure and in addition the Vedic Aditi and Skandamātā who dates back to ancient times.

So it’s a complete course of sādhanā in these four pages of the book—and there is no other book as comprehensive in sādhanā. At the same time, even in Devī Māhātmya, there’s not as much philosophy as there is in this book. In the Devī Māhātmya you have a lot of stories about the Devī and her victories.

But this text goes directly into the mantras and sādhanā, so therefore it is very essential for you to progress in sādhanā. Plus, it’s very easily accessible, being printed in any copy of the Devī Māhātmya. Some of the top singers in India have also sung it with really sweet voices. But just because it is easily accessible, you shouldn’t think it doesn’t have all the esoteric mantras.

Swami Vidyāraṇya in his Yatidaṇḍaiśvarya Vidhāna identifies the Navārṇa mantra presented here as the essence of all the five āmnāyas. He concludes that the Navārṇa mantra eventually belongs to the Western transmission (paścimāmnāya). In essence, the central mantra taught in the Devī Māhātmya, following the Sarvāmnāya system, falls under the stream of Kubjikā.

Additionally, in the most complex mantras of Guhyakālī, she is repeatedly invoked as Cāmuṇḍā, the central deity invoked in the Navārṇa mantra. Likewise, the final word of the mantra, “vicce, ” is itself a deity form in the circle of Śāmbhava Vidyās, the utmost teaching coming from the order of Kubjikā.

If visualization begins with the most basic form of hrīṃ, the heart mantra of the Goddess, it culminates with the pristine form of Mahā Tripurasundarī. This, in essence, provides the framework for the order of Sarvāmnāya. The Devī Atharvaśīrṣa is packed with mantra. It is packed with visualization. It is the essence of Śākta philosophy, Śākta non-dualism, and that is why I thought you should actually learn it.

There are deeper dimensions of the book than it may seem, and you should be encouraged to explore the meaning. Ācārya Sthaneshwar Timalsina — Ācārya Sthaneshwar Timalsina, February 2, 2025
entries.commentary_en:
1. There are innumerable very colorful and insightful stories throughout Hindu spirituality in which the deities competitively seek to determine which deity is superior. This competition gradually prompts them to reflect upon what the ultimate reality is—and to approach that ultimate for answers. Here, the deities approach the Goddess, reminding us of the story told first in the Kena Upaniṣad (3.1–4.4) and expanded in the Devī Bhāgavata Purāṇa (12.8.8–86) in which a humbled Agni, Vāyu, and Indra turn to Devī for instruction. Having been asked by the deities who she is, what her nature is, Devī responds here on two levels. On the first level, she provides her response in ātmastuti format (known in scholarship as an “aretalogy”), in which she details her own qualities. Perhaps the most famous example of an ātmastuti is the Vibhūti Yoga of the Bhagavad Gītā (Chapter 10) in which Śrī Kṛṣṇa similarly details all his divine qualities. As we will see throughout the ātmastuti, Devī’s qualities are not simplistic. She encompasses not one quality in contrast to and to the exclusion of its opposite, but instead she subsumes the entire system of paired opposites within herself. She reigns atop the cosmological hierarchy, but also pervades the hierarchy to render above and below as ultimately equal. She embodies the totality, while standing behind it as its very foundation. When Devī describes “aham, ” however, she is not just describing herself. Rather—on the second, higher level—she is describing the absolute nature of the Self. The Goddess sees that everything, including all pairs of opposites and all positions in the cosmos, is located within the “I am, ” the divine self-consciousness. (For more on the all-encompassing nature of aham, see Tantrāloka 3.200–208.) In this way, the text can be read simultaneously in devotion to the greatness of the Goddess and in recognition that this greatness is also that of our own consciousness. It is for this reason that the āgamas proclaim Devī as śaivī mukham: the very gateway through which we recognize our Śiva-consciousness (Vijñāna Bhairava Tantra 20).

2. This emphasis on recognition is reflected in how Upaniṣad Brahmayogin (1700s CE) interprets the final line of Verse 2 on Devī’s cosmos being “both empty and non-empty” in his commentary on the Devī Atharvaśīrṣa. He cites a profound four-quarter verse whose first half and last half are drawn from different locations, primarily in the Mokṣopāya and its later redaction, the better-known Yogavāsiṣṭha. In particular, the first half appears in Mokṣopāya (4.36.22ab), Yogavāsiṣṭha (4.54.22ab), and Mahopaniṣad (5.184cd), while its last half appears in the Mokṣopāya (6.11.37ab), Yogavāsiṣṭha (6.11.32cd), and Varāha Upaniṣad (2.22ab). The verse reads: “Just as (yathā eva) this (idam) sky (nabhas) is empty (śūnya), so too (tathā eva) indeed ( hi) is the cosmos (jagat) empty (śūnya). To one who does not know (ajña), the cosmos (jagat) is comprised of (maya) a torrent (ogha) of suffering (duḥkha), but to one who knows (jña), it is comprised (maya) of bliss (ānanda). ” When read alongside their fuller context, these verses present a coherent and compelling understanding of how Devī transcends dichotomies and why recognition matters, which threads throughout Upaniṣad Brahmayogin’s broader commentary. Why are the sky and cosmos empty? The sky (nabhas) and the cosmos (jagat) alike are empty because they arise (uttha) from thought constructs (vikalpa) made of (maya) what is not real (asat) (Yogavāsiṣṭha 4.54.22). Once consciousness turns towards thought constructs, it starts to see objects as if they were separate from itself, making those objects denser and more substantive in the mind, which ultimately only causes suffering (see Mahopaniṣad 5.178–183). So what to do then? The answer is direct: “Having cut off all mental activity (chittvā), stay established (tiṣṭha) in your own self (svātman)! What’s (kim) so hard (duṣkara) about that?” (Mahopaniṣad 5.184) After all, the world is as empty as the sky. Furthermore, “Just like (yathā) the quality of emptiness (śūnyatva) resides (sthā) in the sky (nabhas), so too (tathā) does this (idam) [cosmos] reside within Brahman: appearing in the form (rūpa) of real (sat) and unreal (asat) things (vastu), or perhaps (vā) without (na) any form (rūpa) whatsoever (kaścit)” (Mokṣopāya 6.100.38; Yogavāsiṣṭha 6.96.35cd–36ab). That is, when the thought constructs that give rise to the world are cut off, the world is recognized not as something independent, but as residing within Brahman, one’s own pure consciousness, which is the fundamental basis underlying what is real, unreal, and formless. This recognition—that consciousness has no “other, ” that there is no counterpart standing outside of consciousness, separate from it—is what transforms life from suffering to bliss. Liberation is a matter of recognizing the ever-present nature of consciousness, rather than trying to rework thought constructs. When resting as pure consciousness, all seemingly substantial objects are seen to be empty constructions and come to rest within consciousness, which is itself not empty, but is rather the blissful basis of emptiness. This profound understanding sets the stage for invoking Devī as the consciousness which witnesses emptiness (śūnya-sākṣiṇī) in Verse 24—and, indeed, informs Upaniṣad Brahmayogin’s ultimate advice for putting the Devī Atharvaśīrṣa into practice (see Note 53).

entries.title: Ātmastuti: Devī Replies
entries.transliteration: sā abravīd-ahaṃ brahma-svarūpiṇī | mattaḥ prakṛti-puruṣātmakaṃ jagat | śūnyaṃ cāśūnyaṃ ca || 2 ||
entries.translation: She (sā) replied (abravīt): “I am (aham) the very form (svarūpiṇī) of Brahman. From me (mattaḥ), [emerged] this entire cosmos (jagat), comprising (ātmaka) material nature (prakṛti) and pure consciousness (puruṣa), which is both (ca) empty (śūnya) and (ca) not empty (aśūnya) .” Ātmastuti: Devī’s Reply Begins

entries.title: Ātmastuti: Devī Subsumes All Dichotomies I
entries.transliteration: aham-ānandānānandau | ahaṃ vijñānāvijñāne | ahaṃ brahmābrahmaṇī veditavye | ahaṃ pañca-bhūtāny-apañca-bhūtāni | aham-akhilaṃ jagat || 3 ||
entries.translation: “I am (aham) bliss (ānanda) and misery (anānanda). I am (aham) knowledge (vijñāna) and ignorance (avijñāna). I am (aham) to be known (veditavya) as the transcendent reality (brahman) and the immanent reality (abrahman). I am (aham) the five elements (pañcabhūta) and what is beyond the five elements (apañcabhūta). I am (aham) the totality (akhila) of all that exists (jagat) .”
entries.commentary_en:
3. In the first four lines of this verse, Devī identifies with both poles of a seeming dichotomy, where the privative prefix “a-/an-” before the latter word in the dichotomy signifies the absence of the former: she is both ānanda and anānanda (bliss and non-bliss), vijñāna and avijñāna (sound and unsound knowledge), brahman and abrahman (higher and non-higher reality), and pañcabhūta and apañcabhūta (the five elements and the non-five elements). In the fifth line, she then summarizes that she is the entire perceivable cosmos—including within her all its dichotomies without negating the opposing poles. That is, she does not deny the difference between the two sides of the dichotomy, while still including both within her.

4. The pañcabhūta (five elements) are pṛthvī (earth), ap (water), tejas (fire), vāyu (air) and ākāśa (space) that are the tattvas that constitute the outermost limits of manifestation into materiality— making that which is beyond those elements as the innermost core, which is pure consciousness. From a yogic perspective, these elements—and that which is beyond them—are directly engaged with during bhūtaśuddhi practice, for instance. From a tantric perspective (as taught in the Śaiva Siddhānta Kālottara cycle of āgamas, for instance), the five elements from earth to space correspond to the mantric body of Sadāśiva, being associated with Sadyojāta, Vāmadeva, Aghora, Tatpuruṣa, and Īśāna, respectively. This fivefold structure organizing the elements replicates itself at successively higher levels in the tattvas all grouped in fives (from the sensory elements, faculties of action, faculties of perception, mind to puruṣa, kañcukas, etc.), such that these elements can be understood as pervading the totality up to the very end of Śakti— leaving the Śiva tattva as the transcendent principle beyond even these pervasive elements (see Tantrāloka 11.14–21). From the Advaita Vedānta perspective, Upaniṣad Brahmayogin invokes quintuplication theory as described in the eponymous Pañcīkaraṇam attributed to Śaṅkarācārya and commented on by his disciple Sureśvara. In pañcīkaraṇa theory, which bridges between the subtle and gross states of existence, the five elements exist first in an uncompounded and subtle (sūkṣma) state, which is closer to their sensory qualities in consciousness (e.g., subtle earth is closer to smell, subtle space is closer to sound). Then these subtle elements split apart and recombine to form gross (sthūla) composite elements. Each element first divides into two equal halves, and one of those halves divides again into four, so each gross element is composed one-half of its corresponding subtle element and one-eighth of each of the other four elements. The process is called quintuplication as the five initially uncompounded subtle elements become gross composites that each contain all five elements. It is the gross elements that constitute the gross bodies and their seemingly external material universe. For Upaniṣad Brahmayogin, the five elements (pañcabhūta) of this verse refer to the gross elements and what is beyond the five elements (apañcabhūta) refers to the subtle elements. In this theory, Devī thus encompasses both the gross material universe and the underlying subtle elements which cause them, both cause and effect. Whether we follow this fivefold quintuplication of Advaita Vedānta or the fivefold organizing structure of Śaiva tantra in understanding the tattvas, we learn to trace the outermost limits of manifestation into materiality back toward their fundamental source in consciousness—and see every stage of this entire process as being the very expression of the Goddess.

entries.title: Ātmastuti: Devī Subsumes All Dichotomies II
entries.transliteration: vedo ’ham avedo ’ham | vidyā ’ham avidyā ’ham | ajā ’ham anajā ’ham | adhaś cordhvaṃ ca tiryak cāham || 4 ||
entries.translation: “I am (aham) the absolute knowledge (veda) and I am (aham) the phenomenal knowledge (aveda). I am (aham) knowledge (vidyā) and I am (aham) ignorance (avidyā). I am (aham) the unborn (ajā) and I am (aham) that which is born (anajā). I am (aham) below (adhas), above (ūrdhvam), and (ca) across (tiryak) .”
entries.commentary_en:
5. This verse’s dichotomies can be seen as somewhat more nuanced than those of the prior verse. For instance, “veda ” and “aveda” can refer to two different domains of knowledge (absolute knowledge and phenomenal knowledge, respectively), rather than knowledge and its absence. Upaniṣad Brahmayogin accordingly understands them in terms of Devī encompassing both the Sanskrit-language spiritual texts and the texts on mundane subjects in everyday Prakrit language. Similarly to “veda ” and “aveda, ” when we see “vidyā” and “avidyā, ” we need not understand “avidyā” as simply entailing ignorance. The enigmatic verses of the Īśāvāsya Upaniṣad (verses 9–11) instead portray vidyā and avidyā as necessary to jointly cultivate in the attainment of immortality (“vidyāṃ cāvidyāṃ ca yastadvedobhayaṃ saha | avidyayā mṛtyuṃ tīrtvā vidyayāmṛtamaśnute”). Commentators have interpreted these verses differently (e.g., Śaṅkarācārya interprets them in terms of meditative knowledge and ritual action, respectively). Though this interpretation of (a)vidyā is not read into the translation itself, it remains open for contemplation as we reflect upon the nuances of these verses.

6. Through the “ajā” and “anajā” dichotomy, Devī refers to herself as unborn and not-unborn. Although it may seem this way at first, to be “unborn” is not to be something that is unreal, akin to an impossibility which does not exist. Rather, to be unborn means to be hyper-real: something which never came into a particular delimited mode of immanent existence, which never began and will never cease, and thus something that truly exists in a truly autonomous manner that is not contingent upon or conditioned by time/space.

7. In the prior verse, we saw that Devī subsumes within herself all the conceptual opposites. Here we see that she subsumes within her all the directions: above, below, and across (“tiryak” can also mean outwards). She extends infinitely in all directions, pervading and encompassing all in every spatial way. This spatial omnipresence refers not only to what is above and below us, but further to the realms that are above and below the entire earthly realm in which we now reside (see Tantrāloka 8 for a mapping of this deśādhvan, or path of space).

entries.title: Ātmastuti: Vāk Sūkta I
entries.transliteration: ahaṃ rudrebhir vasubhiś carāmi | ahamādityair uta viśvadevaiḥ | ahaṃ mitrāvaruṇāvubhau bibharmi | aham-indrāgnī aham-aśvināvubhau || 5 ||
entries.translation: I (aham) move about (carāmi) through the Rudras [deities of the intermediate realm] and the Vasus [deities of the terrestrial realm]. I (aham) am with the Ādityas [deities of the heavenly realm] and (uta) the Viśvadevas [grouping of deities]. I (aham) sustain (bibharmi) both (ubha) Mitra and Varuṇa. I (aham) [sustain] Indra [king of deities] and Agni [the fire deity]. I (aham) [sustain] both (ubha) the Aśvins [twin deities].
entries.commentary_en:
8. This verse and the next two verses closely parallel the Vāk Sūkta of the Ṛgveda (10.125), which was seen by the female sage (ṛṣikā) Vāk Āmbhṛṇī. Verse 5 reproduces Ṛgveda 10.125.1, Verse 6 draws on and expands 10.125.2, and Verse 7 draws on 10.125.2, 3, and 7. The Vāk Sūkta is also known as the Ṛgvedoktaṃ Devī Sūkta in order to distinguish it from the Tantroktaṃ Devī Sūkta, which is another name for the Aparājitā Stotra of the Devī Māhātmya which appears in Verse 8. To minimize any ambiguity between these two sūktas, the translation and explanatory notes in this book refer to them consistently as the Vāk Sūkta and Aparājitā Stotra.

9. Vedic commentator Sāyaṇa (1300s CE) extolls Vāk Āmbhṛṇī, the seer of this verse, incredibly highly. In his commentary on Ṛgveda (10.125), he identifies her as having realized Brahman (brahmaviduṣī) so completely that by revealing this sūkta, she offered praise (astaut) to her own Self (svātman)! Thus, as Sāyaṇa interprets the verses, he sees the “aham” as pertaining both to the Goddess and to Vāk Āmbhṛṇī, the seer of this verse. Because she became of the same form (tadrūpā) as Brahman, it is also she who moves about through the Rudras (10.125.1), being indistinguishable from Devī herself. And when Devī talks cosmologically in Verse 7 about her source in the waters below (10.125.7), Sāyaṇa reads that “source” more biographically as also being her father Ambhṛṇa in one interpretation (see Note 24). Though Vāk Āmbhṛṇī is extolled so highly, it is not because she attained something that we cannot. It is instead our highest potential to become as indistinguishable from Devī as was Vāk Āmbhṛṇī.

10. Here, Devī unfolds her identification with the entirety of the Vedic cosmos, as symbolized in its 33 core deities: 8 Vasus, 11 Rudras, 12 Ādityas, and 2 Aśvins. The names of these deities and even some of the ordering vary from one text to another. For instance, in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, the final two are not the Aśvins but Indra and Prajāpati, whereas in other cases, like in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 4.5.7.2, Prajāpati is beyond the 33 deities, as the 34th. But what matters especially for us in this text is not the specific enumeration of all these deities, but rather gaining an intuition as to what these deities as a totality mean, in terms of their symbolism.

11. The meaning of these 33 deities, and their numbers, is complex and highly symbolic. It will not be possible to unfold all of these meanings here, so only a few directions for further study are offered. In the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (6.1.2.6–8), the triad of Vasus, Rudras, and Ādityas is situated within the process by which Prajāpati creates the worlds and populates them with beings. Summarizing across several accounts, we can make sense of the triadic structure here. The Vasus are placed on the terrestrial earth (as attendants of Indra, related to the elements of nature), the Rudras are placed in the intermediate sky (as attendants of Śiva who represent the fearful aspects of nature related to the fierce wind), and the Ādityas are placed shining in heavenly space (as solar deities). As such, this triad spans the three realms often described in Vedic cosmology (bhūḥ, bhuvaḥ, svaḥ). This early triad also sets the stage for the chronologically later triad, central to today’s living Hinduism, of Brahmā as grandfather of the Vasus, Śiva as lord of the Rudras, and Viṣṇu as chief among the Ādityas. (This later triad is also included as the very form of Devī in Verse 17, where she is invoked as “brahma-viṣṇu-rudra-rūpiṇī”.) A deeper exploration of these 33 deities occurs within a famous event recounted in several texts, including the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 11.6.3.1–11, Jaiminīya Brāhmaṇa 2.76–77, and Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.1–9. A brief composite version of these recountings appears here with some differences between the texts placed in parentheses. The philosopher-king Janaka of Videha performed a great sacrifice, which was attended by many sages who assembled in his court. Always in pursuit of brahmavidyā (i.e., knowledge of Brahman), he offered a prize of a thousand cows, each with ten pieces of gold tied to their horns, to the sage who best knew the truth. At that very time, the great sage Yājñavalkya told his disciple to bring the cows to his hermitage, boldly claiming the prize before any debate had even begun. This action led to the other sages posing a series of questions to him, to see whether Yājñavalkya did, in fact, best know the truth of all the sages assembled in the court. In this series, Vidagdha Śākalya posed a question: “How many deities are there?” In their back-and-forth, Yājñavalkya puzzlingly offers multiple answers: three hundred and three, three thousand and three, thirty-three, six, three, two, one-and-a-half, and one. When further questioned, Yājñavalkya explains his answers. The hundreds and thousands are not really deities, but are manifestations of the energies of the thirty-three deities. The thirty-three deities are 8 Vasus, 11 Rudras, 12 Ādityas, Indra, and Prajāpati. The 8 Vasus are the earth (Pṛthvī), fire (Agni), wind (Vāyu), intermediate space (Antarikṣa), sun (Āditya), heavenly space (Dyaus), moon (Candramas), and star-constellations (Nakṣatrāṇi). The Vasus are so named because “vas” means to dwell or reside, implying an abode in which something is situated—and it is in these eight substances that the universe is situated. The 11 Rudras refer to the ten senses (or the ten prāṇas) in the body along with the mind (or the ātman). The Rudras are so named because “rud” means to cry or wail, and when the senses/prāṇas and mind/ātman leave the body upon physical death, it leads to wailing of those who cared for a person. The 12 Ādityas are the twelve months as tracked in the movements of the sun. The Ādityas are so named because “ā-dā” means to carry away, and the sun’s movement through its 12 months carries everything and everyone along with them, causing all to go (yanti). (For more on the names of the Ādityas, see the next note.) Yājñavalkya further explains that Indra is thunder and Prajāpati is the yajña sacrifice (in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka account) or that Indra is speech and Prajāpati is the mind (in the Jaiminīya account). The 6 deities are 8 Vasus aside from the moon and constellations—as fire (Agni), earth (Pṛthvī), wind (Vāyu), intermediate space (Antarikṣa), sun (Āditya), and heavenly space (Dyaus) together encompass all the deities. The 3 deities are the three worlds because all deities dwell in these worlds (see above in this note, on bhūḥ, bhuvaḥ, svaḥ). The 2 deities are food and breath (or day and night in the Jaiminīya). The 1.5 deity is the wind because in him the whole world grows— with Yājñavalkya here cleverly playing on a linguistic similarity between the words for “one-and-a-half” (adhyardha) and “grew” (adhyārdhnot). And the 1 deity is Brahman (which he associates with prāṇa in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka), the basis beyond which he warns that no further questioning is possible. So, in this way, we must appreciate how the Vedic cosmology described here is deeply symbolic and links together into a holistic vision the world, our bodies, and the relationship between the two. For instance, if Devī moves about through the Rudras (which have their symbolism in our embodied senses) and the Vasus (symbolizing the elements), then she is the enlivening force of all that we experience, every bit as much within our internal body as in the external cosmos. (See the final note, where we return to this concept.)

12. The Ādityas are first mentioned in the Ṛgveda with a twelvefold list appearing in the Brāhmaṇas and in later texts. The Ādityas also have varying names across texts, but common names also referenced in this Devī Atharvaśīrṣa include: Varuṇa, Mitra, Bhaga, Tvaṣṭṛ, Pūṣan, Indra, Viṣṇu (in his Vāmana avatāra), and others.

13. The Viśvadevas are an all-encompassing term for all the deities of the universe appearing first in the Ṛgveda. For instance, when we make fire libations to the Viśvadevas during homa, then by virtue of the term’s all-inclusiveness, we can ensure we did not miss making offerings to any deity whatsoever.

14. Devī further identifies herself as sustaining three sets of deities, each of which is a common pairing in the Vedic cosmology: Mitra and Varuṇa, Indra and Agni, and the Aśvins. Mitra and Varuṇa are presented as a dvandva (pair) in the Ṛgveda who serve to maintain ṛta (the cosmic order). In the later Brāhmaṇas, they are related with the sky, with Mitra associated with the day and Varuṇa the night: the former preserving order in its more visible social sense and the latter in its less visible cosmic sense. Indra and Agni are two of the most invoked Ṛgvedic deities (alongside Soma, who appears in the next verse). Indra is chief among the Vedic deities, as their king, wielding the thunderbolt (vajra) as his weapon. Agni is of the form of fire—existing on earth as fire, in the atmosphere as lightning, and in space as the sun. This allows Agni to serve as a messenger across the three realms, such that the sacrificial fires during homa become a means by which humans on earth can communicate with the deities at the higher realms. And Indra is the lord of those deities who receives offerings and enacts the divine power. The Aśvins are youthful twin deities who ride upon horses that never tire, and who are guardians of humans in all sorts of troubles they might find themselves in: bringing aid to humans and removing afflictions from them. They are accordingly associated with medicine and healing.

15. Sāyaṇa in his Atharvaveda commentary (Śaunaka recension, 4.30.1) discusses the “aham” through which Devī associates herself with all the above deities. He explains that the I-making activity (ahaṅkāra) that generates self-identifications (abhimāna) is a specific (viśeṣa) modification (vṛtti) of the underlying inner instrument (antaḥkaraṇa), which is formed from (pariṇāma) pure (viśuddha) sattva by nature (rūpa). Thus, just because a particular self-identification may be with something delimited does not mean that the underlying self therefore enters into those limits. A self that is undivided (anavacchinnā) could still take on the appearances of division, which function merely as adventitious adjuncts (upādhi) rather than truly dividing that self. This is, he suggests, indeed the case here with Vāk Āmbhṛṇī, who is of the nature of Brahman, but still identifies herself with various delimited deities like the Vasus, Rudras, Ādityas, and so on. It is like how a mother-of-pearl can mistakenly appear to be silver without actually losing its underlying identity as mother-of-pearl to become silver. Without the mother-of-pearl, there would be no silver appearance, so the latter depends on the former, while the former is independent of the latter. So too with the unlimited self and its delimited identifications.

entries.title: Ātmastuti: Vāk Sūkta II
entries.transliteration: ahaṃ somaṃ tvaṣṭāraṃ pūṣaṇaṃ bhagaṃ dadhāmi | ahaṃ viṣṇum-uru-kramaṃ brahmāṇamuta prajāpatiṃ dadhāmi || 6 ||
entries.translation: I (aham) hold within me (dadhāmi) Soma [the lunar deity], [and the solar deities like] Tvaṣṭṛ [the divine artisan], Pūṣan [the divine guide], and Bhaga [the giver of wealth]. I (aham) hold within me (dadhāmi) Viṣṇu who takes wide strides (urukrama) [in his Vāmana form, as one of the Ādityas], [and the deities associated with creation:] Brahmā, and (uta) Prajāpati.
entries.commentary_en:
16. In some lists (see Note 10), placed above the 33 Vedic deities of the prior verse is Prajāpati as the 34th deity (Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 4.5.7.2). Prajāpati also becomes closely associated with Brahmā, the deity of creation—and across his different origin stories, Prajāpati is seen as a divine progenitor. As a divine progenitor, he plays a role in co-creating the universe with the Goddess Vāc after being born from the Hiraṇyagarbha (the golden embryo) in Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 6.1.2.6–9, 11.1.6.1–2, which is discussed in Verse 7.

17. Of these Ādityas, Tvaṣṭṛ is famous for forging the vajra (thunderbolt), which is the weapon of Indra. And, etymologically, Pūṣan is the one empowered to give puṣṭi (causing people to thrive) and Bhaga is the one empowered to give bhāgya (bringing good fortune).

18. In his commentary on Verse 6, where Bhaga is first mentioned, Upaniṣad Brahmayogin cites the well-known definition of “bhaga” as entailing six excellences (i.e., that characterize the Lord, bhagavat), which the Viṣṇu Purāṇa (6.5.74) lists as: aiśvarya (sovereignty), vīrya (valor), yaśas (renown), śrī (prosperity), jñāna (wisdom), and vairāgya (dispassion).

19. The invocation of Viṣṇu’s urukrama epithet evokes the cosmic stride motif celebrated throughout the Vedas (see Ṛgveda 1.22.17–21; 1.154.1–6; 1.155.5), which the tradition further comes to understand in terms of his Vāmana avatāra or dwarf form (e.g., Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 1.2.5.1–7) and in relation with Bali (e.g., Rāmāyaṇa Bālakāṇḍa 1.29.4–21; Bhāgavata Purāṇa 8.18–23). This dwarf form is placed fifth in the common daśāvatāra list (of the ten forms in which Viṣṇu has incarnated). A composite telling of this story is as follows. In his dwarf form, Viṣṇu requested from Bali, who was conducting yajñas for the lower asuras, just enough land to take three steps, so he could construct a fire altar to perform yajñas for the higher deities. After this request was granted, Viṣṇu grew in size from his dwarf form to such an immense size that in just three strides, he encompassed all the cosmos. It is for this reason that this avatāra of Viṣṇu is also known as Urukrama (far-stepping one) and Trivikrama (one who takes three strides). This entire event is rich in symbolism (e.g., Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 1.9.3.8–10), and the threefold steps can be understood to include the terrestrial earth, intermediate sky, and heavenly space as space (see Note 11), the sunrise, meridian, and sunset as time, the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep as states of experience.

entries.title: Ātmastuti: Vāk Sūkta III
entries.transliteration: ahaṃ dadhāmi draviṇaṃ haviṣmate suprāvye yajamānāya sunvate | ahaṃ rāṣṭrī saṅgamanī vasūnāṃ cikituṣī prathamā yajñiyānām | ahaṃ suve pitaram-asya mūrdhan-mama yonirapsvantaḥ samudre | ya evaṃ veda | sa daivīṃ sampadam-āpnoti || 7 ||
entries.translation: I (aham) bestow (dadhāmi) prosperity (draviṇa) upon the one who makes the ritual offerings (haviṣmat), the one who sponsors the ritual (yajamāna), the one who is worthy of protection (suprāvye), and the one who presses out (sunvat) [the soma during the ritual]. I (aham) am the sovereign (rāṣṭrī) who brings together (saṅgamanī) all the Vasus [deities of the terrestrial realm], the one who knows (cikituṣī) [all], foremost (prathama) among those to be worshiped (yajñiya). I (aham) give birth to (suve) the father (pitṛ) of all this (asya), [placing him] at the head (mūrdhan) [of the cosmos]; my (mama) womb (yoni) is in the water (ap) [below] within (antar) the [primordial] ocean (samudra) [of creation, from which all emerges]. Whoever (yaḥ) knows (veda) thus (evam) attains (āpnoti) the divine qualities (daivī sampad).
entries.commentary_en:
20. In this verse, Devī is associated with the full spectrum of the Vedic yajña (sacrifice): she is those who play a role in its performance, it is she who assembles the deities receiving the sacrifices, and who brings about their intended results. She justifies Vedic ritual while denying the idea that the ritual works in an impersonal manner, without her involvement (e.g., as espoused in the early Mīmāṃsā adṛṣṭa/apūrva theory). As Sāyaṇa notes in his commentary on this verse as it appears in Ṛgveda 10.125.2, a similar idea is articulated by Bādarāyaṇa in his Brahma Sūtra (3.2.38) “phalam ata upapatteḥ,” which Śaṅkarācārya further elaborates in his commentary. Namely, the fruits of actions logically must come from Brahman, rather than impersonally, as espoused in adṛṣṭa/ apūrva theory.

21. For more on the pressing of soma in ritual context, see the description of Soma Pavamāna in the Ṛgveda (9.1–114). In it, the soma is brought forth from plant stalks by being pressed with stones (grāvan), passed through a wool filter (pavitra), prepared through specific recipes that combine soma with either milk (in which case, the drink is called gavāśir), yogurt (dadhyāśir), or barley (yavāśir), and then used in the appropriate ritual context (e.g., as an offering to the deities). This entire process is done not only literally, but also symbolically, as the spiritual meaning of soma is not reducible to that of the plant (see Ṛgveda 10.85.3).

22. In his commentary, Sāyaṇa stays closer to the literal meaning of this verse as describing the Vedic soma ritual: with “suprāvye” indicating one who brings excellent offerings that satisfy the deities, “sunvate” being the one who presses the soma, and “draviṇa” referring to wealth in the form of the fruits of the ritual. Upaniṣad Brahmayogin, in contrast, symbolically interprets the verse’s inner meditative aspects, often through interpretive etymologies (nirvacana). To interpret “suprāvye, ” he begins by defining “suprāvyāya” as “one whose mental disposition (āśaya) is virtuous (śobhana) and uplifted (prakṛṣṭa), whose mind (citta) is inclined (pravaṇa) inward (pratyak) [toward the Self]. ” “Pravya” he then interprets as “the defiled mind (duṣṭa citta), which disperses outward (vyeti) with great intensity (prakarṣa) and thus perishes (naś), ” such that a suprāvya becomes “one from whose virtuous mind (śobhana citta) that [defiled mind] has departed (pragam). ” Then, in his reading, “sunvate” is glossed as “stunvate, ” one who sings praises to the Goddess as she actually is (yathāvat). His reason for placing emphasis on having a virtuous mental disposition and praising the Goddess in truth becomes clear because “draviṇa” is not the fruit of a ritual for him. Rather, it is that the Goddess will bestow wisdom (jñāna) or riches (dhana) to a person, depending on their state of mind (bhāva), making it critical to cultivate the right mental disposition when worshipping her. A mind turned externally may only receive monetary riches, whereas a mind turned inwards will receive the true wealth of knowledge. In this way, we can see two distinct readings of the same verse, each of which is internally consistent and both of which, when taken together, provide a richer understanding of Devī’s teaching.

23. In the third line, Devī provides an enriched understanding of the Hiraṇyagarbha cosmology, developed across the Ṛgvedic sūkta of the same name (10.121), the Matsya Purāṇa (2.25–32), and the Upaniṣads. In one telling, after cosmic dissolution, the self-originated one (svayambhū) arose from the unmanifest and entered the primordial waters in the form of a golden egg, which burst forth into the cosmos with the heavens (svarga) above and the earth (pṛthvī) below. Here, Devī completes the story, by providing the other perspective. Her womb is within those very primordial waters, which serve as the creative matrix in which the egg is nurtured, and it is she who is the generative power which lifts the father of all from the waters when the golden egg bursts forth, and who places him at the head of the cosmos. This line has inspired some extensive and insightful commentaries, which are presented in Notes 24 and 25 below.

24. Sāyaṇa substantially enriches our understanding of this highly symbolic line—whose terms like father (pitṛ), source (yoni), waters (ap), and ocean (samudra) all convey multiple meanings. Sāyaṇa accordingly offers six alternate interpretations of this single line: three in his commentary on the line as it appears in the Ṛgveda (10.125.7) and three as it appears in the Atharvaveda (Śaunaka recension, 4.30.7). Although he is fairly elliptical in explaining each interpretation and silent on why he offers so many, with time and contemplation, a profound logic emerges. The interpretations across his two commentaries follow a common pattern, shifting where the “ocean” is located in relation to the three realms (see Note 11). Namely, the “ocean” can be located in Brahman giving rise to the heavenly realm, on the terrestrial realm with Vāk at its very summit, or in the intermediate realm embodied as deities. Sāyaṇa’s two commentaries provide distinct nuances into each of these realms and are thus presented together in sets. It is noteworthy too that across both commentaries, all the verses he cites to support his interpretations are drawn from recensions of the Yajurveda. To understand what it means for Devī to “give birth to the father of all this, ” Sāyaṇa tends to draw on verses like “heaven is the father” (“dyauḥ pitā”) from the Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa (3.7.5.4–5) and “space came into being from the ātman” (“ātmana ākāśaḥ sambhūtaḥ”) from the Taittirīya Upaniṣad (2.1.1). In the first Ṛgvedic interpretation, the manifest cosmos beginning with the heavenly realm and space element is an effect that emerges from Brahman as its cause. The pure consciousness (caitanya) of Brahman is the “ocean” because it is from that consciousness that all living beings (bhūtajāta) flow forth, as fluctuations (vṛtti) of its mind-water (dhī). And because everything flows from her as fluctuations of her, Devī both causes and pervades the totality—just like threads cause and pervade a cloth. Sāyaṇa’s first Atharvavedic interpretation differs primarily in describing the father and heaven in more personified and mythologically rich Purāṇic terms. That is, pure consciousness gives rise to the creator deity Brahmā who resides in the heavenly realm of Satyaloka, which is the topmost realm of the manifested cosmos when the threefold structure of bhūḥ, bhuvaḥ, svaḥ is expanded into a sevenfold structure of higher realms (ūrdhvaloka). To support the ocean as referring to Brahman, the cause and pervader of the cosmos, Sāyaṇa draws on the verse “the ocean (samudra) is indeed (eva ) its (asya) relative (bandhu), the ocean (samudra) its source (yoni)” from the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (10.6.4.1) and Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad (1.1.2). This first set of readings thus reveals Devī in a more Advaita light. As Brahman, she is the cause of the higher realms, the subtle elements, and even the creator deity Brahmā himself. And by taking māyā as her body (deha), she touches all the fluctuations that constitute the totality—even the distant heavenly realms. In the second set of readings, the “ocean” moves from Brahman to the terrestrial realm. Sāyaṇa’s second Ṛgvedic interpretation was mentioned previously (see Note 9). In it, Devī is speaking as Vāk Āmbhṛṇī, the historical ṛṣikā, whose source (yoni) is Ambhṛṇa, her father. Vāk Āmbhṛṇī is envisioned here standing at the very summit of the terrestrial realm (bhūloka), bringing forth space itself. The vision of this sage—though herself born of a human father here on the earth—giving birth to the cosmic father of space above is a testament to the depth of her realization, which eliminates any difference between her and Brahman. Her name too is significant, as “vāc” (which can become “vāk” or “vāg” depending on Sanskrit declension and sandhi rules) literally means “speech. ” Sāyaṇa’s second Atharvavedic interpretation thus also concerns “vāc. ” But rather than the historical ṛṣikā Vāk Āmbhṛṇī, he refers here to Vāc, the Goddess of Speech. Vāc will be directly invoked in Verse 10 as symbolized by the gladdening cow, through whom all creatures speak and are nourished. But here, Sāyaṇa emphasizes her deep connection with Agni, the fire deity. Vāc is accordingly depicted in terms of fiery energy (tejas). This energy, which is her source (yoni), exists as an underwater fire (vāḍava) that burns beneath the ocean on the terrestrial realm and as lightning (vaidyuta) in the intermediate realm. The underwater fire is an incredibly rich symbol of barely-contained energy, which first appears in the Ṛgveda (8.102.4) and then develops through the story of Aurva as told variously across the Mahābhārata, Harivaṃśa, Śiva Purāṇa, and Skanda Purāṇa. That this energy is present both on the terrestrial realm as fire and the intermediate realm as lightning strongly evokes how Agni manifests in these realms (see Note 14). Sāyaṇa’s own commentary on the Ṛgveda (1.142.9; 10.45.1–3) reveals the close connection between fire and speech, established in the Aitareya Upaniṣad (1.2.4), Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad (1.3.12), and elsewhere. Just as Vāk Āmbhṛṇī stood atop the summit of the terrestrial realm and gave rise to space, so too does the fiery energy of Vāc, the speech goddess, rise from the terrestrial oceans into the sky in lightning form. Sāyaṇa depicts Vāc here as “embodying the form of the ‘middle’ speech” (“mādhyamika-vāg-rūpāyā”). This depiction is not just placing Vāc in the “middle” of the terrestrial and heavenly realms. The “middle speech” (madhyamā-vāk) is a specific stage in the fourfold division of speech in which the subtle and still-undifferentiated impressions start to take form within consciousness, before they manifest outward (see Note 35 for more on the fourfold speech). This second set of readings thus focuses on the fire and power of embodied speech—both in the historical ṛṣikā and in the Goddess—as it rises from the terrestrial realm to the realms above. It is through this fiery energy that she illuminates all worlds and living beings. In the third set of readings, the “ocean” is accordingly located in the intermediate realm (antarikṣa), where “water” constitutes the very bodies (śarīra) of the deities (deva). Such associations with this antarikṣa realm are old ones, as “ocean” (samudra) and “water” (ap) are both listed as synonyms of this realm in the earliest Vedic glossary Nighaṇṭu (1.3)—and Yāska (~700–400 BCE), the grammarian, reminds us not to confuse this atmospheric ocean with the earthly one (Nirukta 2.10). In both of Sāyaṇa’s commentaries, the primordial ocean functions as described throughout the Ṛgveda: its waters bring forth the cosmos, encompass the deities, and protect those who worship them (e.g., 7.49.2, 10.82.6, 10.121.7). Although Sāyaṇa does not offer it, there is precedent too for deities in this realm having “bodies of water. ” Chāndogya Upaniṣad (7.10.1) teaches that water is to be meditated upon because it takes on all forms, including those of the deities. Aitareya Brāhmaṇa (2.16) tells of a dilemma in which every deity desired to be worshiped first. The dilemma was resolved by worshiping water, as thereby all deities felt themselves to have been worshiped. It proclaims: “the waters (ap) are, indeed (vai), all (sarva) the deities (deva). ” On this basis, in the Saṃnyāsa Upaniṣads, water becomes an acceptable substitute to make offerings into for renunciates who cannot offer into fire. The same line of water being all deities is cited again in the context of the Vedic Agnicayana ritual, which establishes correspondences between the fire-altar and the cosmos (Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 10.5.4.14). The opening passage of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad that Sāyaṇa cites to support his first reading develops similar themes in the Vedic Aśvamedha sacrifice, establishing correspondences between parts of the horse and the cosmos itself, which allow the meditator to grasp the manifold totality. The horse’s front and back are the rising and setting sun, its hair the plants and trees, its breath the wind, its mouth the fire (as another connection between Agni and Vāc), and so on, integrating measurements of time, space, and embodiment. Here we find that while the back of the horse is the heavens (“dyauḥ pṛṣṭham”) and the chest below is the earth (“pṛthivī pājasyam”), the belly is the intermediate realm (“antarikṣam udaram”), as the hollow cavity in between (for a parallel line, see Atharvaveda 10.7.32). It is this cosmic being, who represents all microcosmic and macrocosmic correspondences, who is said to have “the ocean as its relative and the ocean its source” as Sāyaṇa cited earlier from the Bṛhadāraṇyaka (1.1.2) and which later gets further reinforced (1.2.3). Whereas Sāyaṇa is informed by Śaṅkarācārya’s commentary on this verse heavily in first set of readings—linking the ocean rather straight to Brahman, thus bypassing any intermediate deities —in this third set, he does not. Brahman here dwells as the consciousness within the deities in this intermediate realm, who are embodied from this primordial water. Sāyaṇa’s third Atharvavedic interpretation differs from his Ṛgvedic interpretation primarily in that there Devī does not merely pervade (vyāpnomi) the cosmos, but more actively inspires, impels, sets in motion (prerayāmi): the same action of inspiring forward that is requested in the “pracodayāt” of the Gāyatrī mantras (like the Mahālakṣmī Gāyatrī taught in Verse 12). This third set of readings thus maintains the manifold embodiments of divine embodied forms, which represent the totality of correspondences between the microcosm and the macrocosm, without losing that Devī guides the very waters from which these deities are formed.

25. Upaniṣad Brahmayogin initially reads Devī not through a language of powe r, as the rāṣṭrī, the queen, who gathers (saṅgamanī) up the Vasus, but rather through spatial language as having the form of the realm (rāṣṭrarūpiṇī) within which the Vasus move and operate. He does this by interpreting “saṅgamanī” through gamanīya (able to be entered) and saṃcaraṇīya (able to be moved about within)—calling back to his earlier depiction of Devī as the self that supports everything (sarvādhārātman) in his Verse 5 commentary. Then, when he interprets how she gives birth to the father in this line, he builds on this spatial language to articulate a different language of her power. He treats Devī not as being located “at the [spatial] head” (mūrdhan) at the very hierarchical top of the cosmos, but glosses it as “I am the head” (mūrdhā aham) at the beginning of the cosmos: the equilibrium state of the three guṇas (guṇa-sāmyātman) which is the unmanifest causal state of prakṛti from which the differentiated universe comes forth (see Bhāgavata Purāṇa 11.22.12). This solidifies her power in a more thorough manner than if she were just queen over the Vasus: she is now the fundamental support from which the individual selves (jīva) and even (api) the father (that is, Īśvara, otherwise seen as the progenitor) alike emerge. Upaniṣad Brahmayogin makes this case by citing a phrase from heard scripture (śruti), “jīveśāvābhāsena karoti, ” which affirms that Devī (as māyā) creates both Īśvara and jīva as differentiated appearances (ābhāsa) (Nṛsiṃha Uttaratāpanīya Upaniṣad 9.3). This verse from scripture offers a clearly non-dualist account where pure consciousness precedes the differentiation between the Lord and the individual, thus eradicating any fundamental distinction between them as being due to illusion. This non-dualist account carries forward from this line into Upaniṣad Brahmayogin’s unique gloss on the next line, as he transitions from cosmology to soteriology. Rather than reading Devī’s womb as being in the water within (antar) the ocean (samudra), he reads it as “antaḥ samudre, ” an “inner ocean” associated with the lotus-shaped physical heart (puṇḍarīkākāra-māṃsapiṇḍa). This inner ocean’s waters flow (udravati) perfectly (samyak) within (antar) the heart (hṛd) of all (sarva) living beings (prāṇin)—as well as in the material world, in the form of the five elements (pañcabhūta) which all contain some water in pañcīkaraṇa theory (see Note 4). Thus, Devī’s nature (svarūpa) is present in both the individual (jīva) and Lord (Śiva). One who knows this (ya evaṃ veda) attains the true state of the Goddess (devī-pada), whose nature (rūpa) is pure consciousness (cit) which is common (sāmānya) to all beings. In this way, Upaniṣad Brahmayogin transforms a verse about Devī’s place atop the cosmic hierarchy into a different kind of verse: a verse that still maintains Devī’s supremacy, while granting ultimate equality to all beings on the hierarchy (even the Lord and bound subjects), because all beings emerge from and abide within her pure consciousness.

26. The daivī saṃpad (divine qualities) are those qualities which are conducive to liberation, whereas the āsurī saṃpad are those that lead to bondage. As enumerated in the Bhagavad Gītā—whose 16th chapter (Daivāsura Saṃpad Vibhāga Yoga) is dedicated to distinguishing between these two sets of qualities—the daivī saṃpad entail 26 divine qualities: abhaya (fearlessness), sattvasaṃśuddhi (purity of heart), jñānayogavyavasthiti (steadfastness in the yoga of knowledge), dāna (charity), dama (self-control), yajña (sacrifice), svādhyāya (study of sacred texts), tapas (self-discipline), ārjava (sincerity), ahiṃsā (nonviolence), satya (truthfulness), akrodha (absence of anger), tyāga (renunciation), śānti (peacefulness), apaiśuna (absence of slander), dayā bhūteṣu (compassion for all beings), aloluptva (freedom from greed), mārdava (gentleness), hrī (modesty), acāpala (steadiness), tejas (vigor), kṣamā (patience), dhṛti (fortitude), śauca (purity), adroha (freedom from malice), and nātimānitā (absence of excessive pride) (16.1–3).

entries.title: The Deities Revere Devī: Aparājitā Stotra
entries.transliteration: te devā abruvan – namo devyai mahādevyai śivāyai satataṃ namaḥ | namaḥ prakṛtyai bhadrāyai niyatāḥ praṇatāḥ sma tām || 8 ||
entries.translation: The (te) deities (deva) replied (abruvan): “Reverence (namas) to the Goddess (devī), the Great Goddess (mahādevī). Constant (satatam) reverence (namas) to her, the auspicious one (śivā). Reverence (namas) to she who is nature (prakṛti) and the granter of good fortune (bhadrā). Indeed (sma), we bow down (praṇata) and remain disciplined (niyata) to her (tām) .” Taking Shelter in Devī as Durgā
entries.commentary_en:
27. This verse begins the Aparājitā Stotra of the Devī Māhātmya (5.9–82), such that the deities respond to Devī’s ātmastuti describing herself from the Ṛgveda with a hymn of praise from the Devī Māhātmya. It is this seamless blending together of traditions that makes this text an embodiment of the Goddess herself: powerful and all-encompassing.

28. This verse and the next four verses appear in an analogous section of the Devī Gītā (1.44–48), an important section of the Devī Bhāgavata Purāṇa, where the deities revere the goddess with great devotion. That this five-verse sequence is replicated with only minimal differences in this later work shows the immense influence of the Devī Atharvaśīrṣa on the development of Śākta philosophy, practice, and devotion.

29. We can understand namaḥ (and all etymologically related “nam” words like namaskāra, praṇāma, etc.) as including, but also going beyond reverence. As Ācārya Kṣemarāja explains in his commentary on the Svacchanda Tantra (2.16), “praṇāma” takes the form of entering into (anupraveśa) the essential nature (svarūpa) of the Supreme (para), which emerges (unmagna) through the state of bowing down (prahvībhāva) of the body (śarīra) and so on (ādi). Ācārya Abhinavagupta provides a deep examination of the meaning of “namaḥ” at the start of his Īśvarapratyabhijñā-vivṛti-vimarśinī, where he comments upon the maṅgalaśloka of Ācārya Utpaladeva’s vivṛti, which gives reverence to the one who is the essence (ātman) of the course of the world (loka-yātrā) in its entirety (aśeṣa), which has been manifested (avabhāsita) by his own will (sva-icchā) alone. What could “namaḥ” mean in relation to something so profoundly all-inclusive and expansive? To begin with, Abhinavagupta rejects the notion that it is the mere recitation of the sound “namaḥ” that matters. Namaḥ is not, he says, analogous to a song that pleases a deity just by the deity hearing it being pronounced. Nor is it just some sort of noun-like substantive (sattvarūpa). When we say “namaḥ śivāya, ” we do not mean that we offer the word “namaḥ” to Śiva. Rather, the word has a meaning and this meaning indicates what it is that we actually offer. This is why “namaḥ” is used with a dative (like Śivāya), as it offers something to a deity: rather than just being a sound that one makes, it has a meaning that pertains to that deity. And what “namaḥ” means is not just a word at the level of speech, but something that simultaneously involves the mind, speech, and body, according to the well-known triad discussed in the āgamas, where reverence is not only about the mind and speech, but also expressed by prostrating with the body. When one beholds the transcendent excellence of the nature of the supreme consciousness (bhagavatsvarūpotkarṣa) during sādhanā, one’s body, breath, and mind are automatically dissolved within the supreme. Yet, upon the time of arising from sādhanā (i.e., vyutthāna), one’s ingrained latent impressions (saṃskāra) that one is merely the body, breath, and mind can return, causing identification with this rather limited form of subjectivity (māyāpramātṛ), rather than the higher subjectivity of the supreme consciousness. What “namaḥ” indicates, therefore, is the “bowing down” that is submerging one’s identification with their mind, breath, and body through absorption (samāveśa), as one enters into their true identity as the foundational subjectivity (pradhānapramātṛ), such that one recognizes who they really are. It is this, rather than just the utterance of words or physical gestures, that constitutes the real reverence (namaḥ) to the supreme.

entries.title: Taking Shelter in Devī: Durgā Sūkta
entries.transliteration: tām agni-varṇāṃ tapasā jvalantīṃ vairocanīṃ karma-phaleṣu juṣṭām | durgāṃ devīṃ śaraṇaṃ prapadyāmahe ’surān nāśayitryai te namaḥ || 9 ||
entries.translation: Unto her (tad), who has the hue (varṇa) of fire (agni), blazing (jvalantī) with heat (tapas), radiant like the sun (vairocanī), Goddess Durgā (durgā devī), who is gratified (juṣṭa) by the fruits of our actions (karmaphala): in your shelter (śaraṇa), we arrive (prapadyāmahe). Reverence (namas) to you (te), the destroyer (nāśayitrī) of asuras.
entries.commentary_en:
30.
