This verse adapts the invocation which appears in the Durgā Sūkta of the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka (10.2) of the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda, in its final section (which is known as the Mahānārāyaṇa Upaniṣad or Yājñikī Upaniṣad) as well as in the Ṛgveda’s Rātrī Khila (4.2.12), which are the supplemental mantras appended to the Rātrī Sūkta of the Ṛgveda proper (10.127), which was seen by sage (ṛṣi) Kuśika Saubhara or female sage (ṛṣikā) Rātri Bhāradvājī.

31. One may wonder why Durgā is blazing with tapas—which means not only heat, but also the heat generated by austerities. Why would Durgā need to perform any austerities? One answer, suggested by the verse itself, is that she’s gratified by the fruits of her devotees’ actions, in which case she may be blazing through the heat of our tapas, which we offer to her, rather than her own tapas. But this answer alone does not exhaust the potential meanings here. In his commentary on this verse—as it appears within the Devī Gītā (1.45) (see Note 28)—Nīlakaṇṭha Śaiva (1700s CE) provides an insightful answer as to what it might mean for Durgā herself to perform tapas. He does so by citing the Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad (1.1.8–9). To set the stage, the Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad centers around the householder Śaunaka’s profound question to ṛṣi Aṅgiras: “What is that by which, if known, all else becomes known?” (1.1.3). Knowledge, Aṅgiras reveals, has a higher and a lower modality. The lower entails knowledge of the Vedas and their limbs (like grammar, astronomy, etc.) and the higher entails realization of the all-pervading, subtle, immutable source of the totality: Brahman. Just like the spider expands out its web from within, so too does that immutable source expand out the universe entirely from within itself. But how? “By tapas, Brahman expands... ” (“tapasā cīyate brahma...” 1.1.8) these mysterious verses proclaim, which then describe Brahman’s tapas to be of the nature of knowledge (“... jñānamayaṃ tapaḥ” 1.1.9). More specifically, Brahman’s tapas is knowledge of the sequence of creation through which it expands itself into the totality. We can understand this process in light of the commentarial tradition of Śaṅkarācārya, including his subcommentator Ānandagiri and Upaniṣad Brahmayogin. Like a swelling seed about to sprout or like a parent swelling with joy at the first news of pregnancy, Brahman expands. Brahman expands first into the unmanifest condition of māyā, in which the three guṇas are held in equilibrium and the latent impressions of all beings (saṃskāra) are at rest. Because this unmanifest condition is common to all beings as the experience they “consume” in order to manifest, it is described symbolically as food (anna). Desiring to bring forth the totality, Brahman then expands into immanent manifestation where it takes the form of the Hiraṇyagarbha in the realm of māyā (see notes to Verses 6–7), described as life itself (prāṇa). The Hiraṇyagarbha is the primordial seed from whose sprouting emerges the collective mind (manas), the five elements that extend this mind into materiality (described as truth; satya), the multiple worlds (loka) formed from those five elements, and, ultimately, the action (karma) that individual beings perform in these worlds, whose results are enduring, thus described as undying (amṛta). Underlying this vast expansion is Brahman’s tapas. Unlike creator deities like Prajāpati, who create through effortful tapas, Brahman’s tapas is effortless as it consists of knowledge. It is through the knowledge of the sequential process of creation that the Hiraṇyagarbha, name (nāma), form (rūpa), and the symbolic food emerge. Creation is not effort, but a byproduct of all-knowingness of the universal Brahman. And, even as this universal Brahman creates particular objects of knowledge within the realm of māyā, its knowledge of all these objects of creation yields neither effort nor pain: as knowledge is the modification of māyā in which sattva guṇa predominates. Within this commentarial tradition—and its tapas of knowledge, through which Brahman comes to create all and comes to know all of its creation—we see a form of tapas suitable to the highest divinity. Perhaps it is through such a tapas that Durgā blazes.

32. Nīlakaṇṭha Śaiva offers a further fascinating and unique interpretation of this verse: treating it as a mantroddhāra (i.e., the uddhāra or “extraction” of an esoteric mantra that is encoded secretly in a text) for the Devī Praṇava Mahāmantra (which is more explicitly encoded in Verse 18). He begins by interpreting the “varṇa” of “agni-varṇām” not as “hue, ” but as its other prominent meaning of “letter, ” such that Durgā no longer appears visually with the hue of fire but, rather, her mantra sonically contains the letter of fire (which is known to be raṃ), giving him the letter “r.” One encoding of raṃ within fire is explained in Note 46. At another point in his decoding of this verse, Nīlakaṇṭha cites the Prapañcasāra as an authority. It is thus worth noting that this text too places the vyāpaka class of consonants (3.2), and r in particular as a member of that class (3.71), as having the nature of fire. Thus, the r/fire association is secured. Next, Nīlakaṇṭha renders the “tapas” of “tapasā-jvalantīṃ” as the letter ī, such that Durgā’s mantra blazes forth with ī, rather than Durgā blazing forth with heat (see Note 31). How does he derive ī from tapas? The Devī Gītā (2.9), the text he is commenting upon, provides the first step: names of Devī’s power are given there to include both tapas and māyā, alongside several others: tamas (darkness), jaḍa (insentience), jñāna (knowledge), pradhāna (primordial matter), prakṛti (nature), śakti (power), and ajā (unborn). (Some of these same names appear also in this Devī Atharvaśīrṣa.) After linking tapas with māyā as a first step, he then links māyā with “ī” in the second step. Although Nīlakaṇṭha does not supply a canonical source, other texts like the Sītā Upaniṣad explicitly state that “māyā is spoken of as the letter ‘ī’” (māyā īkāra ucyate). As the Sītā Upaniṣad itself and its commentary by Upaniṣad Brahmayogin make evident, this ī/māyā connection is one that concerns how the unmanifest causal power gives rise to the totality. This connection is supported not only by the Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad which Nīlakaṇṭha cites, where māyā plays this role especially in the commentarial tradition of Śaṅkarācārya (see Note 31), but also within the Devī Gītā itself, which links ī with the causal body of the Goddess (4.42). This ī/māyā connection provides the second key for his decoding. Finally, Nīlakaṇṭha interprets “vairocanīṃ” not as indicating that Durgā’s appearance is radiant like the sun, but rather that her mantra possesses the letter “h.” To do so, he draws on the literal definition of “virocana” as the sun. Prapañcasāra, read alongside its Vivaraṇa commentary attributed to Padmapāda, associates the sun with bindu and the moon with visarga (3.7). In Sanskrit grammar, bindu is the “drop” placed atop a phoneme to nasalize it (ṃ) and visarga is the “emission” of a voiceless aspiration (ḥ). But it is critical to remember that in Hindu thought, the cosmos emerges from and is governed by a fundamental grammar. As such, bindu and visarga are not merely grammatical, but help bridge between the domains of grammar and cosmology. As the Prapañcasāra (3.65) explains, bindu (ṃ) consists of puruṣa (pure consciousness) and is the tattva (element) from which ha manifests, so ha wears the bindu atop its head, manifesting as haṃ (हां). And visarga (ḥ) consists of prakṛti (material nature), which manifests as sa, to produce saḥ (साः). Thus, by linking the sun (virocana) from the verse to bindu, Nīlakaṇṭha retrieves both ha and ṃ. He now has all the keys to decode the mantra and assemble ha, r, ī, and ṃ into the Devī Praṇava Mantra of hrīṃ. Having understood Durgā’s fiery hue, her blazing with tapas, and her sun-like radiance in mantric rather than visual terms, Nīlakaṇṭha accordingly renders the final line of this verse: “I (aham) take shelter (śaraṇa) in Durgā, who is the embodiment (rūpiṇī) of the māyā-bīja [hrīṃ]. ” That Nīlakaṇṭha discovered this tantric mantra encoded in a Vedic verse—which it seems went unnoticed for some two-and-a-half thousand years between the first appearance of this Vedic mantra and his commentary in the late 1700s—is a testament to the incredible continuity and considerable ingenuity of Hindu thought. It is perhaps for this reason that Nīlakaṇṭha even seems to refer to the Devī Atharvaśīrṣa as the Hṛllekhā Upaniṣad (i.e., the esoteric teaching of the hrīṃ mantra) in his commentary on the Devī Gītā (10.22). It is worth returning to a theme raised in the above mantra decoding, but which was not fully developed there, and which would be useful to develop now (see Prapañcasāra 4.17–21). The theme is the haṃ of puruṣa and saḥ of prakṛti. As the macrocosmic universe and the microcosmic person alike are combinations of these two principles of puruṣa and prakṛti, we can combine their two manifestations haṃ and saḥ in one way to get haṃsa. The word “haṃsa” translates to “swan” in Sanskrit, where the swan was long seen as a symbol of not only the breath, but ultimately the ātman (Self). This is owing to the observable ability of swans to float upon the water without their feathers getting soaked—and the mythic ability of a certain type of swan to separate out the milk from a mixture of milk adulterated with water. Both abilities symbolize purity, transcendence, and discernment. In the other combination, following the relevant Sanskrit rules for combining words (visarga sandhi), saḥ and ahaṃ become so’haṃ. The word “so’haṃ” translates to “I am He” and is a verbal recognition that one is, in truth, the highest divinity. And when s and h are removed from “so’haṃ, ” and the relevant Sanskrit rules for combining words (pūrvarūpa sandhi) are applied, then what remains is oṃ, the divine vibration that pervades existence itself. Thus, we see that either way of combining the phonemes of puruṣa and prakṛti and even their subsequent withdrawal from their combined form yields divinity alone. It is through such procedures that we see the close correspondences between grammar and cosmology. Without straying too far from the present text, which grounds itself so heavily within sādhanā, it is perhaps also important to note that these are not idle speculations, but directly implicate sādhanā. After all, haṃsa and so’haṃ are the famous ajapa (unrecited) mantras, so named because we need not recite them with our voices, because we are all constantly reciting them on each and every breath. That is, if we listen closely, we can hear the tones of haṃ and saḥ in our inhalations and exhalations. This practice is described frequently in yogic texts—but receives special depth of attention in the commentary by Śivopādhyāya (1700s CE) on the Vijñāna Bhairava Tantra (verses 154–156). He shows how the bindu and visarga can be located yogically in different parts of the yogi’s body, including the heart and dvādaśānta (twelve fingerbreadths from the body) and explains when the first combination of haṃ for exhalation and saḥ for inhalation (haṃsa) will transform into the haṃ for inhalation and saḥ for exhalation (so’haṃ), among innumerable other insights. In this way, grammar and cosmology become embodied, and we see how all modes of understanding the Goddess can resonate in harmony.

33. Upaniṣad Brahmayogin’s text varies from ours in several locations. This verse is one such instance that is worth discussing, as his verse ends with “durgāṃ devīṃ śaraṇamahaṃ prapadye sutarāṃ nāśaya te tamaḥ” which might be read as a puzzling request for Durgā to destroy “her” darkness. Clarifying what is meant here, Upaniṣad Brahmayogin offers her a prayer: “For my sake (mat-kṛte), completely (sutarām) destroy (nāśaya) the darkness (tamas) comprised of (ātmaka) not seeing (adarśana) you (yuṣmad). ” Thus the darkness “of” Durgā is not her own darkness, but the darkness which makes us unable to see her. This prayer is one that speaks to all of us, who deeply desire to behold our beloved Goddess.

entries.title: Calling Forth Devī as Vāc
entries.transliteration: devīṃ vācam-ajanayanta devās tāṃ viśva-rūpāḥ paśavo vadanti | sā no mandreṣam-ūrjaṃ duhānā dhenur-vāg-asmān-upa suṣṭutaitu || 10 ||
entries.translation: The deities (deva) brought forth (ajanayanta) the Goddess (devī) of Speech (vāc), and every (viśva) form (rūpa) of creature (paśu) communicates (vadanti) through her (tāṃ). May she (sā)—the melodious (mandrā) cow (dhenu) of speech (vāc), milking (duhānā) for us (naḥ) sustenance (iṣ) and vitality (ūrj)—come (etu) close (upa) to us (asmān), being well-praised (su-stutā).
entries.commentary_en:
34. This verse is from the Ṛgveda (8.100.11) seen by the sage (ṛṣi) Nema Bhārgava.

35. It is not difficult to see in this verse an early understanding, which would become important to Trika Śaivism: that speech has levels from gross and manifest to increasingly subtle. The fourfold division of speech—which can be seen as the four legs of the cow of speech mentioned here—was first described in Ṛgveda (1.164.45), a verse seen by Sage Dīrghatamas. This verse reveals that the articulated speech of humans is that which moves, whereas the other three types of speech remain secret and do not stir. Commentaries on this verse, from the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (~700–600 BCE), through centuries of grammarians like Yāska (~700–400 BCE), Patañjali (~200 BCE), Bhartṛhari (~500 CE), and Nāgeśa Bhaṭṭa (1700s CE), and Vedic commentator Sāyaṇa (1300s CE) reveal a diversity of interpretations. A common theme is that there is a level of manifest speech that is used by the paśus (or bound beings) in their ordinary everyday dealings (vyāvahārika)— and others that are used in a religious context or by other animals whose speech is not externally articulated, but rather resides internally. That is, our most common use of speech does not recognize Vāc in her most pristine, subtle form. As the depth of interpretation of this verse develops, particularly by Sāyaṇa, it comes to receive a properly Śaiva tantric interpretation—along the lines of Ācāryas Utpaladeva and Abhinavagupta—in which these four forms of speech correspond to the parā (supreme), paśyantī (seeing), madhyamā (middle), and vaikharī (articulated) levels, where each of these levels is, in turn, embodied: beginning with the mūlādhāra (root) cakra, moving upward from the nābhi (navel) to hṛdaya (heart) to the organs of articulation such as the palate, lips, etc. (tālvoṣṭhādi). This enriched understanding of this verse, and the fourfold structure of speech, provides a powerful continuity between these Vedic verses and the oral teachings given to Sarvāmnāya initiates today on mantra practice.

entries.title: Bowing to Diverse Forms of Devī
entries.transliteration: kālarātrīṃ brahma-stutāṃ vaiṣṇavīṃ skanda-mātaram | sarasvatīm-aditiṃ dakṣa-duhitaraṃ namāmaḥ pāvanāṃ śivām || 11 ||
entries.translation: To Kālarātrī, who is praised (stutā) by Brahmā, Vaiṣṇavī, the mother (mātṛ) of Skanda, Sarasvatī, and Aditi [mother of the Ādityas], the daughter (duhitṛ) of Dakṣa, we bow down (namāmaḥ) to she who purifies (pāvanā), she who is auspicious (śivā).
entries.commentary_en:
36. Mahākālī is praised by Brahmā in the Brahmastuti of the Devī Māhātmya (1.73–87), which is also known as the Tantrokta Rātri Sūkta where he further lists her instruments (e.g., “khaḍginī śūlinī ghorā gadinī cakriṇī tathā | śaṅkhinī cāpinī bāṇa-bhuśuṇḍī-parighāyudhā”) in 1.80–81.

37. We can see here the śaktis of the common triad of Hinduism today (see Note 11), with Mahākālī (the śakti of Śiva, i.e., Mahākāla), who was praised by Brahmā, Vaiṣṇavī (Viṣṇu’s śakti), and Sarasvatī (Brahmā’s śakti). When paired with Skandamātā and Aditi, the daughter of Dakṣa (see Verse 13), we have a fivefold structure of mothers in these seven names. It could be possible to extract other such structures. For instance, Nīlakaṇṭha Śaiva interprets Skandamātā as Pārvatī (Śiva’s śakti) to form his triad of śaktis in his Devī Gītā commentary (1.47). When one consults rare sources like the earliest versions of the Skanda Purāṇa, however, Skandamātā has a much longer history that suggests she may be better positioned, like Aditi, as a separate figure, rather than as being situated within the common triad.

entries.title: Mahālakṣmī Gāyatrī
entries.transliteration: mahālakṣmyai ca vidmahe sarva-śaktyai ca dhīmahi | tanno devī pracodayāt || 12 ||
entries.translation: We contemplate (vidmahe) and (ca) set our minds (dhīmahi) upon Mahālakṣmī, who embodies all (sarva) the powers (śakti). May that (tat) Goddess (devī) guide us (naḥ) forward (pracodayāt).
entries.commentary_en: 38. This is the Gāyatrī of Mahālakṣmī. “Gāyatrī” is a type of meter with 3 pādas of 8 syllables each, following the meter of the famous and revered Ṛgvedic mantra (3.62.10) to Savitṛ. There is a range of adhikāra (qualifications) required to practice mantras. Receiving the Devī Atharvaśīrṣa from a qualified ācārya can be understood to give one the adhikāra to recite the Mahālakṣmī Gāyatrī, as a form of sāmānya dīkṣā (general initiation), because this full mantra is spoken by the ācārya and heard by the student. In contrast, other mantras like the Navārṇa and Pañcadaśākṣarī are given only in code, and thus will require specific initiations into those systems. Hearing and receiving the Devī Atharvaśīrṣa alone is not sufficient. In Sarvāmnāya, these specific initiations are given in a krama-dīkṣā, that is, a sequence of initiations into each of the āmnāyas (tantric transmissions). The sequence begins with the samaya dīkṣā, where one receives the rules and procedures that form the foundation of the path along with the first initiatory mantra to be practiced until advancement to the next initiation. Both the Navārṇa and Pañcadaśākṣarī mantras are included within this sequence of initiations in the Sarvāmnāya.

entries.title: Hymn to Devī as Aditi
entries.transliteration: aditirhyajaniṣṭa dakṣa yā duhitā tava | tāṃ devā anvajāyanta bhadrā amṛtabandhavaḥ || 13 ||
entries.translation: Aditi indeed (hi) was born (ajaniṣṭa) as your (tava) daughter (duhitṛ), O Dakṣa! And from (anu-) her (tāṃ), those auspicious (bhadra) deities (deva), in the lineage (bandhu) of immortality (amṛta), [i.e., the Ādityas] were born (-ajāyanta).
entries.commentary_en:
39. This verse is from the Ṛgveda (10.72.5) which was seen by Bṛhaspati Āṅgirasa, Bṛhaspati Laukya, or Aditi Dākṣāyaṇī.

40. Upaniṣad Brahmayogin, in commenting on Verses 11–13, emphasizes a common principle. He first describes Kālarātrī as the night of dissolution of “anything that appears (bhāna) as being separate from (atirikta) oneself (sva). ” And, as the deities recognize that they arose from Aditi, he renders their appeal to that from which Aditi arose as such: “Having considered (man) that we (vayam) are your daughter’s sons (dauhitra), free (muc) us (asmān) from the delusion (bhrama) of existence (astitva) being separate from (atirikta) oneself (sva). ” These glosses continue a central theme of his commentary: overcoming the false notion of separate existence (see Note 2). We are not limited subjects wandering in an independently existing objective realm. Objectivity is rather simply an externalized mode of our most fundamental subjectivity, which is not the limited ego, but the very aham, the I-am, that is the Goddess herself.

entries.title: Mantroddhāra of the Pañcadaśākṣarī
entries.transliteration: kāmo yoniḥ kamalā vajra-pāṇir- guhā hasā mātariśvābhram-indraḥ | punar-guhā sakalā māyayā ca purūcyaiṣā viśva-mātādi-vidyom || 14 ||
entries.translation: [The phoneme of] desire (kāma) [ka], [the phoneme shaped like a] womb (yoni) [e], [the phonemes of the] lotus (kamalā) [i.e., Lakṣmī] [ī], [the] bearer-of-the-thunderbolt (Vajrapāṇi) [i.e., Indra, whose phoneme is] [la], [the] hidden one (guhā) [hrīṃ]; [the phonemes] ha and sa (hasā), [of the] wind deity (Mātariśvan) [ka], cloud (abhra) [ha], lord of deities (Indra) [la], and again (punar) the hidden one (guhā) [hrīṃ]; [the phonemes] sa-ka-la (sakalā), and (ca) together with [the] magical power (māyā) [phoneme] [hrīṃ]: this (eṣā) [mantra of ka-e-ī-la-hrīṃ, ha-sa-ka-ha-la-hrīṃ, sa-ka-la-hrīṃ] is to be abundantly (puru) recited (ucyā) as the primordial (ādi) knowledge (vidyā), the mother (mātṛ) of the universe (viśva). Oṃ.
entries.commentary_en:
41. This verse contains the mantroddhāra (i.e., the uddhāra or “extraction” of an esoteric mantra that is encoded secretly in a text) for the Pañcadaśākṣarī Mahāmantra (the great fifteen-lettered mantra) of the Śrīvidyā. The keys to the uddhāra are filled in brackets but the mantra can only be practiced upon initiation into this system. Upon initiation, this mantra is discovered to be particularly replete with meaning. In fact, the Yoginīhṛdaya (2.15–16) as illuminated by Amṛtānanda’s (1300s CE) commentary provides six overlapping and mutually enriching ways of understanding the mantra, in terms of its essential nature, meaning transmitted within tradition, concealed meaning, and so on. For the distinctions between Amṛtānanda’s Hādi tradition and the Kādi tradition, where the mantra is explained in Bhāskararāya’s Varivasyā Rahasya (57–59 and onward), see the following Note 42.

42. This mantroddhāra verse is widely cited in later works— often with unclear attributions. Aside from the Devī Atharvaśīrṣa, this verse also appears in the Tripurā Upaniṣad, a concise 16-verse text that scholars date after 1500 CE. It may be worth exploring from which of these two texts this important verse is being cited— and why that might be the case. Bhāskararāya Makhin (1690–1785 CE) is the author who perhaps cites this verse more than any other: typically to unpack and advocate for the Kādi tradition (in which the great fifteen-lettered mantra begins with the ka phoneme, in distinction to the Hādi tradition, in which it begins with ha). Bhāskararāya is certainly well aware of the Devī Atharvaśīrṣa, as he cites it in at least three locations in his Guptavatī commentary on the Devī Māhātmya. First, in his opening discussion on Navārṇa mantra where he draws a mantra extraction from Verse 20. Second, in his commentary on Devī Māhātmya (5.7), where he notes that the first verse of the Aparājitā Stotra (“namo devyai mahādevyai... ”) also appears here (Verse 8). And third in his commentary on the Prādhānika Rahasya, which is an ancillary to the Devī Māhātmya that examines the cosmological process whereby the primordial matter is differentiated through the three guṇas. In it, Devī is described as with and without defining signs (lakṣyālakṣyasvarūpā). To support his understanding of alakṣyā, with Devī having no signs through which she could become an object of cognition, he cites Verse 23. He does not, however, provide a commentary on the Devī Atharvaśīrṣa itself. Bhāskararāya cites this mantroddhāra verse in several of his works: the Setubandha (his signature work which comments upon a section of the Vāmakeśvara Tantra), where in treating verses 1.118–9, he attributes the verse to the Śaunaka recension of the Atharvaveda, in the Varivasyā Rahasya (1.8) (his treatise on Śrīvidyā worship), where he attributes it to the Śāṅkhāyana recension of the Ṛgveda in his autocommentary, and in his Saubhāgyabhāskara commentary on the Lalitā Sahasranāma (1.17), where he attributes it to the Tripurā Sūkta recited by the Atharvavedins. In each of these cases, it is clear that Bhāskararāya is citing this verse with the Tripurā Upaniṣad as his authority because he explicitly cites the text’s name or refers to its properties (like its 16-verse length or its decoding of both Kādi and Hādi mantras). Bhāskararāya also comments on the Tripurā Upaniṣad itself, where he begins by attributing the entire text to the Śāṅkhyāyana belonging to the Śākala school of the Ṛgveda following the Kauṣītaka Brāhmaṇa—with Upaniṣad Brahmayogin similarly associating this text with the Ṛgveda in his commentary. In several places in his commentary on the Tripurā Upaniṣad, Bhāskararāya, however, notes variant readings in other recensions, which either go unnamed (in Verses 11 and 12) or are attributed to the Atharvaveda (in Verses 6, 8, 10, 16). Thus, although Bhāskararāya differs from text to text in which Vedic affiliation he assigns to this verse, even when he is citing an Atharva source, he is citing the Tripurā Sūkta, rather than the Devī Atharvaśīrṣa. We may wonder why this is. It likely has to do with how the Tripurā Upaniṣad first provides the mantroddhāra for the Kādi (in Verse 8) and then provides that of the Hādi (in Verse 9), which Bhāskararāya takes as signifying that, while Śrīvidyā is the most elevated of mantras and all its traditions are ultimately nondifferent, the Kādi tradition has a most favored position and thus it comes first. Of the other references to this verse, the Kāmakalāvilāsa of Puṇyānanda with its commentary by Naṭanānanda also stands out. In his commentary on Verse 11, Naṭanānanda cites this mantroddhāra verse on the authority of the Tripurā Upaniṣad—as he cites both the Hādi and Kādi extraction verses from verses 8 and 9 of that text—which he further ascribes to the Śāṅkhāyana recension of the Ṛgveda (an ascription he repeats while commenting on Verses 15–17). It is noteworthy that while the Kashmir Series of Texts and Studies and the Tantrik Texts Series edited by Arthur Avalon both have the Śāṅkhāyana ascription in the Devanāgarī, Avalon’s English translation inexplicably attributes it instead to the Śaunaka recension of the Atharvaveda. The Kāmakalāvilāsa thus offers two further conclusions. First is to note that Naṭanānanda comes in the Hādi tradition of Śrīvidyā, as an initiate in the illustrious lineage of Puṇyānanda, alongside Amṛtānanda (see Note 41). Yet, he has no qualms in citing the Tripurā Upaniṣad’s extraction of both the Hādi and the Kādi. It appears Bhāskararāya’s interpretation—that the Kādi’s extraction appearing in the verse before the Hādi’s extraction implies the superiority of the former over the latter—is not shared by Naṭanānanda. Thus, whether or not one seeks to favor one tradition over the other, the Tripurā Upaniṣad provides a purely Śrīvidyā text that covers just one āmnāya, but more thoroughly addresses its two traditions—and may thus be a preferable citation over the Devī Atharvaśīrṣa, which covers multiple āmnāyas. Second is that the scholarly dating of the Tripurā Upaniṣad must be pushed earlier by a few centuries. As Naṭanānanda, who cites this text, was likely active during the 1300s CE, it is no longer viable to date this text as post-1500s. That said, this revised chronology would not necessarily overturn the received view that the Devī Atharvaśīrṣa precedes the Tripurā Upaniṣad, as even the 1300s are on the later end of the date range proposed by scholars for the Devī Atharvaśīrṣa, which is from the 800s to 1300s. As the Devī Gītā’s dating is uncertain and likely postdates the revised dating of the Tripurā Upaniṣad, its attestation of the Devī Atharvaśīrṣa offers little help in establishing their relative chronology. Upaniṣad Brahmayogin’s commentary similarly provides little help in establishing a chronology: as a late commentator in the 1700s, he cites and comments on both texts. In his commentary on the Tripurā Upaniṣad, however, he does refer the reader to his Devī Atharvaśīrṣa commentary to learn the Kādi decoding, which could possibly suggest some sort of priority given to the latter. In terms of their content, the evidence is suggestive at best in establishing a chronology. The Hādi extraction verse in the Tripurā Upaniṣad clearly depends on the Kādi verse shared with the Devī Atharvaśīrṣa because it instructs one to take the three root phonemes of the prior Kādi verse (asyā mūlatrikam) and enter into their place (āveśayantaḥ) those of the Hādi. Hence, rather than the Devī Atharvaśīrṣa seeming derivative for having just one of the two Śrīvidyā extractions of the Tripurā Upaniṣad, it rather seems to have the original and more substantial extraction upon which the potentially later Tripurā Upaniṣad depends in order to extract its second mantra.

entries.title: Visualization of Mahā Tripurasundarī
entries.transliteration: eṣātmaśaktiḥ | eṣā viśvamohinī | pāśāṅkuśa-dhanur-bāṇa-dharā | eṣā śrī-mahā-vidyā | ya evaṃ veda sa śokaṃ tarati || 15 ||
entries.translation: She (eṣā) is the power (śakti) of the self (ātman). She (eṣā) is the one who enchants (mohinī) the universe (viśva). Bearing (dharā) the noose (pāśa), goad (aṅkuśa), bow (dhanus), and arrows (bāṇa). She (eṣā) is the great-wisdom-goddess (śrīmahāvidyā). Whoever (yaḥ) knows (veda ) thus (evam) will cross over (tarati) all sorrow (śoka).
entries.commentary_en: 43. Showing her integration into Śrīvidyā, Devī is explicitly identified here as Śrī Mahāvidyā. Following the introduction of her rahasya (esoteric) mantric form in the Pañcadaśākṣarī mantra of Mahā Tripurasundarī in the prior verse, her corresponding iconic visual form is now given in this verse, where she is visualized holding the instruments of a noose, goad, bow, and arrows.

entries.title: Requesting Protection from Bhagavatī
entries.transliteration: namaste astu bhagavati mātar-asmān-pāhi sarvataḥ || 16 ||
entries.translation: Let there be (astu) reverence (namas) to you (te), O Goddess (bhagavatī). Mother (mātṛ), protect (pāhi) us (asmān) in every direction (sarvatas).

entries.title: Enumerating the Forms of Devī
entries.transliteration: saiṣāṣṭau vasavaḥ | saiṣaikādaśa rudrāḥ | saiṣā dvādaśādityāḥ | saiṣā viśvedevāḥ somapā asomapāś ca | She (sā) herself (eṣā) [is] the eight (aṣṭa) Vasus. She (sā) herself (eṣā) [is] the eleven (ekādaśa) Rudras. She (sā) herself (eṣā) [is] the twelve (dvādaśa) Ādityas. She (sā) herself (eṣā) [is] the Viśvedevas: [both] those who drink soma (somapā) and (ca) those who drink what is not soma (asomapā). She (sā) herself (eṣā) [is] the malevolent spirits (yātudhāna), the asuras, the demons (rakṣas), the flesh-eating spirits (piśāca), the demigods (yakṣa), and the perfected masters (siddha). She (sā) herself (eṣā) [is] the [three guṇas or qualities of prakṛti] of light-clarity (sattva), heat-passion (rajas), and darkness-dullness (tamas). saiṣā yātudhānā asurā rakṣāṃsi piśācā yakṣāḥ siddhāḥ | saiṣā sattvarajastamāṃsi | saiṣā brahmaviṣṇurudrarūpiṇī | saiṣā prajāpatīndramanavaḥ | saiṣā grahanakṣatrajyotīṃṣi | kalākāṣṭhādikālarūpiṇī | tām ahaṃ praṇaumi nityam | pāpāpahāriṇīṃ devīṃ bhukti-mukti-pradāyinīm | anantāṃ vijayāṃ śuddhāṃ śaraṇyāṃ śivadāṃ śivām || 17 ||
entries.translation: She (sā) herself (eṣā) [is] the deities of creation (Brahmā), sustenance (Viṣṇu), and destruction (Rudra). She (sā) herself (eṣā) [is] Prajāpati [the creator deity], Indra [the chief of deities], and the Manus [the progenitors of mankind]. She (sā) herself (eṣā) [is] the planets (graha), the star- constellations (nakṣatra), and the celestial bodies (jyotis). She is of the form of (rūpiṇī) time (kāla): [measured in] the digits of the moon [that mark the passage of time] (kalā), the [further] subdivisions of time (kāṣṭhā), and so on (ādi). Her (tām), I (aham) always (nityam) revere (praṇaumi): The Goddess (devī) who is the remover (apahāriṇī) of sins (pāpa) and the bestower (pradāyinī) of worldly enjoyment (bhukti) and spiritual liberation (mukti). Who is without end (anantā), victorious (vijayā), pure (śuddhā), a refuge (śaraṇyā), the giver of peace (śivadā), the auspicious one (śivā).
entries.commentary_en: 44. This verse is an uncompromising enumeration of how Devī is all-encompassing. As it begins, we see again the familiar Vedic cosmology, but extended from the highest levels down to the lowest. She encompasses the three groups of higher deities (the Ādityas of the heavenly realm, the Rudras of the intermediate realm, and the Vasus of the terrestrial realm). She further encompasses the totality of all the deities, the Viśvedevas, including not only those who drink soma (somapā), but also those who drink what is not soma (asomapā). The Aitareya Brāhmaṇa (2.2.8) provides one list of the somapā and asomapā deities, each of which comprises 33 deities. The somapā deities are the 8 Vasus, 11 Rudras, 12 Ādityas, Prajāpati, and Vaṣaṭkāra (who personifies the vaṣaṭ mantra pronounced during yajñas). The asomapā deities listed are the 11 Prayājas, 11 Anuyājas, and 11 Upayājas, which refer respectively to various deities which personify the preliminary (pra-), subsequent (anu-), and supplementary (upa-) offerings (-yāja) made during a yajña. Further down, she encompasses the demigods (yakṣa) and perfected masters (siddha), until encompassing even those figures associated with the lower realm: malevolent spirits (yātudhāna), asuras, demons (rakṣas), and flesh-eating spirits (piśāca). She further subsumes a series of triads encompassing the three guṇas or qualities of material nature (prakṛti), the deities governing creation, sustenance, and destruction (Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra), the progenitors (with Prajāpati as the undifferentiated source of all creation, Indra as its sovereignty over manifest creation, and Manu as the progenitor of its embodiment in humanity), and further triads of astronomy and temporality. She is always revered too as the one who fulfills both goals of sādhanā (spiritual practice): bhukti (material enjoyment) and mukti (spiritual liberation). In short, there is nothing that is not the embodiment of the Goddess. She is śivadā, which, as Note 1 reminds us, means she is the one who bestows our own Śiva-consciousness.

entries.title: Mantroddhāra of the Devī Praṇava
entries.transliteration: viyad-īkāra-saṃyuktaṃ vīti-hotra-samanvitam | ardhendu-lasitaṃ devyā bījaṃ sarvārtha-sādhakam || 18 ||
entries.translation: [The phoneme of] space (viyat)  [ha] combined with (saṃyukta) the phoneme ī (īkāra), accompanied by (samanvita) [the phoneme of the sacrificial] fire (vītihotra) [i.e., Agni whose phoneme is] [ra], and adorned (lasita) with the half-moon (ardhendu) [ṃ] [makes hrīṃ]: the seed (bīja) [mantra] of the Goddess (devī), which accomplishes (sādhaka) all (sarva) of life’s aims (artha).
entries.commentary_en:
45. This verse contains the mantroddhāra (i.e., the uddhāra or “extraction” of an esoteric mantra that is encoded secretly in a text) for the Devī Praṇava Mahāmantra. The keys to the uddhāra are filled in brackets.

46. Initiates have the keys to extract some of these phonemes through bhūtaśuddhi practice, where “raṃ” is the fire phoneme in the navel and “haṃ” is the space phoneme in the throat.

entries.title: Phalaśruti of Devī Praṇava Mantra
entries.transliteration: evam-ekākṣaraṃ brahma yatayaḥ śuddha-cetasaḥ | dhyāyanti paramānanda-mayā jñānāmburāśayaḥ || 19 ||
entries.translation: Those self-restrained ones (yati) who meditate (dhyāyanti) in this way (evam) upon this one-syllable (ekākṣara) Brahman [i.e., hrīṃ] with pure (śuddha) thoughts (cetas) are filled with (-maya) the highest (parama) bliss (ānanda), [and become] oceans (amburāśi) of wisdom (jñāna).

entries.title: Mantroddhāra of Navārṇa
entries.transliteration: vāṅ-māyā brahmasūs-tasmāt ṣaṣṭhaṃ vaktra-samanvitam | sūryo ’vāma-śrotra-bindu-saṃyuktaṣ-ṭāttṛtīyakaḥ | nārāyaṇena sammiśro vāyuś-cādharayuk-tataḥ | vicce navārṇako ’rṇaḥ syān-mahad-ānanda-dāyakaḥ || 20 ||
entries.translation: The [bīja mantra of] speech (vāc) [of Vāgdevī is aiṃ], the [bīja mantra of] magical power (māyā) [is hrīṃ], the creator deity’s son (brahmasū) [is Kāmadeva, the deity of desire, and the bīja mantra of kāma is klīṃ], the sixth (ṣaṣṭha) [letter counting from] that [ka of klīṃ] (tasmāt) [is ca; and ca] endowed with (samanvita) the [nyāsa phoneme of the] mouth (vaktra) [ā, makes cā], [the phoneme of the] sun (sūrya) [ma], [the nyāsa phoneme of the] right (avāma) ear (śrotra) [u] joined together (saṃyukta) with the point (bindu) [ṃ], the third (tṛtīyaka) [phoneme] counting from ṭa [is ḍa] combined (sammiśra) with [the bīja mantra of] Nārāyaṇa [ā, makes ḍā], the [phoneme] of the wind deity (Vāyu) [ya] joined (yuk) with the [nyāsa phoneme of the] lower (adhara) [lip] [ai, makes yai], afterward (tataḥ) is “vicce”: this forms (syāt) the nine-lettered (nava-arṇaka) mantra (arṇa) [aiṃ-hrīṃ-klīṃ-cā-muṇ-ḍā-yai- vic-ce], the giver (dāyaka) of great bliss (mahadānanda).
entries.commentary_en:
47. This verse contains the mantroddhāra (i.e., the uddhāra or “extraction” of an esoteric mantra that is encoded secretly in a text) for the Navārṇa Mahāmantra (the great mantra with nine letters). The keys to the uddhāra are filled in brackets but the mantra can only be practiced upon initiation into this system. More insight about this mantra can be gained by consulting the Guptavatī by Bhāskararāya Makhin, which cites this text to give further meaning to the mantra.

48. Initiates have the keys to extract some of these phonemes, such as the letters contained in different parts of nyāsa practice.

entries.title: Visualization of Bhuvaneśvarī
entries.transliteration: hṛtpuṇḍarīka-madhyasthāṃ prātaḥsūrya-samaprabhām | pāśāṅkuśa-dharāṃ saumyāṃ varadābhaya-hastakām | trinetrāṃ rakta-vasanāṃ bhakta-kāma-dughāṃ bhaje || 21 ||
entries.translation: She who is situated in the center (madhyasthā) of the lotus of the heart (hṛtpuṇḍarīka), with the same luster (samaprabhā) as the morning (prātar) sun (sūrya), bearing (dharā) the noose (pāśa) and goad (aṅkuśa), peaceful (saumyā), displaying the hand gestures (hastaka) of granting blessings (varada) and dispelling fear (abhaya), three-eyed (trinetrā), wearing blood- red (rakta) [colored] garments (vasana), who grants (dughā) the desires (kāma) of her devotees (bhakta)—her, I worship (bhaje).
entries.commentary_en: 49. This is the dhyāna śloka (visualization verse) of Bhuvaneśvarī, one of the Daśa Mahāvidyā deities (ten great-wisdom-goddesses), showing how this text seamlessly moves through the Vedic, Purāṇic, and multiple Tantric sādhanās, integrating them all. Although some systems treat the classical āmnāya systems (like the Śrīvidyā invoked in Verses 14–15) as distinct from the later Daśa Mahāvidyā system (invoked in this verse), tantras of the Sarvāmnāya provide the mappings of the Daśa Mahāvidyā deities onto the classical āmnāya systems. These tantras include the Parātantra, Chinnamastākhaṇḍa of the Śaktisaṅgama Tantra, and Vaḍavānala Tantra. And within the Sarvāmnāya paddhatis (practice manuals), these āmnāya deities are, in turn, further mapped onto Durgā in her 18-armed Ugracaṇḍā form along with her retinue, thus integrating all three major Śākta orders from the earliest to the most recent: Durgā, Āmnāya, and Mahāvidyā. (Ugracaṇḍā with 18 arms, who is so central to Sarvāmnāya, is depicted in a paubha and another painting in this book’s figures.)

entries.title: Reverence to Mahādevī
entries.transliteration: namāmi tvāṃ mahādevīṃ mahābhaya-vināśinīm | mahā-durga-praśamanīṃ mahā-kāruṇya-rūpiṇīm || 22 ||
entries.translation: I revere (namāmi) you (tvāṃ), O Great Goddess (mahādevī), the destroyer (vināśinī) of great fear (mahābhaya), who pacifies (praśamanī) great (mahā) difficulties (durga) [and] is the embodiment (rūpiṇī) of great (mahā) compassion (kāruṇya).

entries.title: Transcendent Names of Devī
entries.transliteration: yasyāḥ svarūpaṃ brahmādayo na jānanti tasmād ucyate ajñeyā | yasyā anto na labhyate tasmād ucyate anantā | yasyā lakṣyaṃ nopalakṣyate tasmād ucyate alakṣyā | yasyā jananaṃ nopalabhyate tasmād ucyate ajā | ekaiva sarvatra vartate tasmād ucyate ekā | ekaiva viśvarūpiṇī tasmād ucyate naikā | ata evocyate ajñeyānantālakṣyājaikā naiketi || 23 ||
entries.translation: Whose (yasyāḥ) true form (svarūpa) even Brahmā and other deities (brahmādi) do not (na) know (jānanti)—she is therefore (tasmād) called (ucyate) “the unknowable” (ajñeyā). Whose (yasyā) end (anta) cannot (na) be found (labhyate)—she is therefore (tasmād) called (ucyate) “the endless” (anantā). Whose (yasyā) distinctive signs (lakṣya) cannot (na) be signified (upalakṣyate)—she is therefore (tasmād) called (ucyate) “the signless” (alakṣyā). Whose (yasyā) birth (janana) cannot (na) be found (upalabhyate)—she is therefore (tasmād) called (ucyate) “the unborn” (ajā). She alone (ekā eva) exists (vartate) everywhere (sarvatra)— she is therefore (tasmād) called (ucyate) “singular” (ekā). She alone (ekā eva) is of the form of the [multifarious] universe (viśvarūpiṇī)—she is therefore (tasmād) called (ucyate) “not- singular” (na-ekā). Indeed (eva), it is for this reason (atas), she is called (ucyate) thus (iti): “the unknowable-endless-signless-unborn-singular- [and]-not-singular” (ajñeyā-anantā-alakṣyā-ajā-ekā-na-ekā).
entries.commentary_en: 50. In Verse 23, Devī is approached in an apophatic manner: describing her through negation, by what she is not. She is not knowable, not with an end, not with a sign, not born, not reducible to one-or-not-one. In Verse 24, Devī is then approached in a cataphatic manner: by describing her through affirmation, by what she is. This verse goes from form to form sequentially, showing how she is the most essential aspect of each form, and this innermost essence is what we proclaim by the name Durgā. We can see here critically important ideas that are developed in more detail elsewhere. For instance, the relations posited here between mantras, phonemes, words, concepts, and consciousness are revealed to have great philosophical and soteriological importance (see, for instance, Tantrāloka 11.54–82). The necessity of reaching and then further transcending the śūnya states of emptiness that constitute the culmination of other paths similarly has great philosophical and soteriological importance (see, for instance, Spandakārikā 1.12–13 with Ācārya Kṣemarāja’s commentary). It is far too common to conflate the consciousness of absence (śūnya) with the absence of consciousness. When we recognize the consciousness who is the witness of emptiness, as this verse recommends, we go beyond these empty states and continue in our process of fully recognizing our Śiva-consciousness.

entries.title: Essential Forms of Devī
entries.transliteration: mantrāṇāṃ mātṛkā devī śabdānāṃ jñāna-rūpiṇī | jñānānāṃ cinmayātītā śūnyānāṃ śūnya-sākṣiṇī | yasyāḥ parataraṃ nāsti saiṣā durgā prakīrtitā || 24 ||
entries.translation: Among mantras, the Goddess (devī) is the phonemes (mātṛkā) [from which mantras are essentially made]. Among words (śabda), she is of the nature (rūpiṇī) of cognition (jñāna) [which senses the essence of words, their meaning]. Among modes of cognition (jñāna), she is that transcendent consciousness (cinmayātītā) [that pervades and grasps all cognitive modes]. Among the void states (śūnya), she is the consciousness who is witness (sākṣiṇī) of those void states (śūnya). Beyond whom (yasyāḥ) there is none (nāsti) superior (paratara): this very goddess (eṣā), she (sā) is proclaimed (prakīrtitā) as Durgā.

entries.title: Reverence to Durgā
entries.transliteration: tāṃ durgāṃ durgamāṃ devīṃ durācāra-vighātinīm | namāmi bhavabhīto ’haṃ saṃsārārṇava-tāriṇīm || 25 ||
entries.translation: To Durgā—the unattainable (durgamā) goddess (devī) who removes (vighātinī) all wrong conduct (durācāra)—being fearful (bhīta) of what I may become (bhava), I offer her (tāṃ) my reverence (namāmi): she is the transporter across (tāriṇī) the ocean (arṇava) of cyclic conditioned becoming (saṃsāra).

entries.title: Phalaśruti of Devī Atharvaśīrṣa I
entries.transliteration: idam-atharvaśīrṣaṃ yo ’dhīte sa pañcātharvaśīrṣa-japa-phalam-āpnoti | idam-atharvaśīrṣam ajñātvā yo ’rcāṃ sthāpayati | śatalakṣaṃ prajaptvā ’pi so ’rcāsiddhiṃ na vindati | śatam aṣṭottaraṃ cāsya puraścaryā-vidhiḥ smṛtaḥ | daśavāraṃ paṭhed yas tu sadyaḥ pāpaiḥ pramucyate | mahā-durgāṇi tarati mahādevyāḥ prasādataḥ || 26 ||
entries.translation: One (yaḥ) who studies (adhīte) this (idam) [Devī] Atharvaśīrṣa receives (āpnoti) the [same] fruits (phala) as the recitation (japa) of five (pañca) Atharvaśīrṣas. One (yaḥ) who establishes (sthāpayati) an image to worship (arcā) without knowing (ajñātvā) this (idam) Atharvaśīrṣa— even (api) after reciting (prajaptvā) [a mantra] a hundred (śata) lakh (lakṣa) [i.e., 10 million] times—will not (na) attain (vindati) success (siddhi) in that worship (arcā). One hundred (śata) plus (uttara) eight (aṣṭa) [i.e., 108] [recitations] of this (asya) [Atharvaśīrṣa] is recalled (smṛta) to be the procedure (vidhi) for preliminary initiatory rites (puraścaryā). One (yaḥ) who would recite (paṭhet) [this Atharvaśīrṣa] ten (daśa) times (vāra), indeed (tu), immediately (sadyas) will be released (pramucyate) from one’s wrongdoings (pāpa). [One] crosses over (tarati) immense (mahā-) difficulties (durga) by the blessings (prasāda) of the Great Goddess (mahādevī).
entries.commentary_en: 51. There are five principal Atharvaśīrṣa texts (corresponding, for instance, to the five deities of Smārta pañcāyatana worship), namely: Nārāyaṇa/Viṣṇu, Rudra/Śiva, Sūrya, Gaṇapati, and our present text for Devī. Upaniṣad Brahmayogin confirms this reference to the five common Atharvaśīrṣa texts beginning with the Nārāyaṇa Atharvaśīrṣa and so on (nārāyaṇādi).

entries.title: Phalaśruti of Devī Atharvaśīrṣa II
entries.transliteration: sāyam adhīyāno divasakṛtaṃ pāpaṃ nāśayati | prātar adhīyāno rātrikṛtaṃ pāpaṃ nāśayati | sāyaṃ prātaḥ prayuñjāno apāpo bhavati | niśīthe turīyasandhyāyāṃ japtvā vāksiddhir bhavati | nūtanāyāṃ pratimāyāṃ japtvā devatāsānnidhyaṃ bhavati | prāṇapratiṣṭhāyāṃ japtvā Reciting (adhīyāna) [this Atharvaśīrṣa] in the evening (sāyam) destroys (nāśayati) all wrongdoings (pāpa) committed (kṛta) during the day (divasa). Reciting (adhīyāna) [this Atharvaśīrṣa] in the morning (prātar) destroys (nāśayati) all wrongdoings (pāpa) committed (kṛta) during the night (rātri). Combining recitation (prayuñjāna) [of this Atharvaśīrṣa] in the evening (sāyam) and in the morning (prātar), one [therefore] becomes (bhavati) [completely] free of wrongdoing (apāpa). Having recited (japtvā) [this Atharvaśīrṣa] at midnight (niśītha)—at the fourth (turīya) junction of the day (sandhyā) [alongside dawn, noon, and dusk]—the perfection (siddhi) of speech (vāc) occurs (bhavati). Having recited (japtvā) [this Atharvaśīrṣa] before a new (nūtana) image (pratimā), the presence (sānnidhya) of the deity (devatā) [within the image] occurs (bhavati). Having recited (japtvā) [this Atharvaśīrṣa] at the installation (pratiṣṭhā) of life (prāṇa) [into the image], the installation prāṇānāṃ pratiṣṭhā bhavati | bhaumāśvinyāṃ mahādevīsannidhau japtvā mahāmṛtyuṃ tarati | sa mahāmṛtyuṃ tarati | ya evaṃ veda | ityupaniṣat || 27 ||
entries.translation: (pratiṣṭhā) of life (prāṇa) occurs (bhavati). Having recited (japtvā) [this Atharvaśīrṣa] in the presence (sannidhi) of the Great Goddess (mahādevī) on [amṛtasiddhiyoga, the astrological combination of] the day of Mars (bhauma) [i.e., Tuesday] and the Aśvinī [lunar mansion], great death (mahāmṛtyu) is crossed over (tarati). One (saḥ) crosses over (tarati) great death (mahāmṛtyu), the one who (yaḥ) knows (veda) thus (evam). Thus ends (iti) the esoteric teaching (upaniṣad).
entries.commentary_en:
52. As noted at the outset of this book, the Devī Atharvaśīrṣa can be recited as part of the process of prāṇapratiṣṭhā, which installs life into a mūrti. For those initiates who are learning this process, this book should be an especially valuable resource.

53. For Upaniṣad Brahmayogin, when the text says “one who knows thus” (ya evaṃ veda) will cross over great death, it is telling us that death can be transcended through contemplation and the grace (prasāda) of Mahādevī. Specifically, he prescribes one to always (sadā) remain intent upon (para) contemplation (anusaṃdhāna) of the Advaita Vedāntic truth: “Brahman—realized (siddha) through the negation (apahnava) of everything (sarva) [other than itself]—is nothing but (mātra) one’s own self (sva), which has no ‘other’ to be a counterpart (niṣpratiyogika). ” This contemplation, done intently, is thus the way to transcend death: one must constantly reject all that is not the Self, only to find that there is nothing that is not the Self.

54. The text indeed closes by promising that we can cross over beyond the great death (mahāmṛtyu). But what exactly is the great death? We see this concept in the Kaṭha Upaniṣad, which provides not only a reflection upon death, but a conversation with Death (Yama) himself. Having left Naciketas waiting at his door, Yama offers him boons to make amends, as any good host should—and, despite being offered all the worldly pleasures and wealth, Naciketas instead requests knowledge of the self (ātman) and what happens after death. In answering this question, Yama teaches: “Whatever (yad) indeed (eva) is here (iha), that (tad) is there [in the beyond] (amutra); whatever (yad) is there [in the beyond] (amutra), that (tad) is likewise (anu) here (iha). One (tad) who (yad) sees (paśyati) as if (iva) there were any difference (nānā) here (iha) goes (āpnoti) from death (mṛtyu) to death (mṛtyu)” (2.1.10). This process of going from death to death is understood as mahāmṛtyu, the great death. This great death brings us back to the all-encompassing “aham” raised in the very first verse uttered by Devī. When Devī describes who she is, she describes herself as embodying and reconciling all the seeming opposites: the conceptual dichotomies, the highest to lowest in space, the past to future in time, and more. Throughout this text, as we have learned Devī’s nature, so too have we learned our own—as she is speaking not just about herself, but about the universal aham which constitutes our innermost nature too. And if we, as Yama states, go beyond seeing only difference (nānā) everywhere, between our lives “here” and “there” in the great beyond, and recover our embodiment of the totality with all its seeming opposites (about the opposites, see Pratyabhijñāhṛdaya 3), then we cross over the great death. And this is why Devī is the very gateway to our own Śiva-consciousness. When Devī is asked who she is (kāsi tvam?) she instead responds to help us remember who we are.
